articles.title_orig: U.S. Intel Warns China's Space-Based Directed Energy Weapons Could Soon Threaten Satellites
articles.title_zh: U.S. Intel Warns China's Space-Based Directed Energy Weapons Could Soon Threaten Satellites
articles.content_orig:
By the end of the decade, China could threaten satellites with space-based directed energy weapons, according to a new report from the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA). This would add a dangerous new anti-satellite (ASAT) capability to Beijing’s arsenal, which already includes ground-based directed energy weapons that can disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites. The report, released Monday, offered another glimpse into what is to come as the potential for conflict in space only continues to grow .
The unclassified DIA report is based largely on open-source information, with a cutoff date of July. It was published to detail growing threats from China, Russia and emerging powers Iran and North Korea to global interests in the space domain. The report’s release also took place as the U.S. is becoming increasingly open about its own ASAT capabilities. Last month, for instance, U.S. military officials acknowledged for the first time that America has weapons in orbit .
“The PLA probably considers DEWs [directed energy weapons] ideal counterspace systems because they can cause both reversible and nonreversible effects against satellites,” the report, titled Challenges to Security in Space , explains. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”
The report did not provide specifics about whether China is developing lasers, high-powered microwaves, particle beams or a combination of these capabilities.
We have reached out to the agency for more information but did not immediately receive a response.
Reversible attacks include efforts to jam satellite signals or temporarily blind their optics. The latter can be done with devices like laser dazzlers .
DIA reported that in 2021 the People’s Liberation Army media “asserted that laser weapons were entering a golden age; they cited dazzling (i.e., temporarily blinding a sensor) as one of the many operational uses of laser weapons.”
Non-reversible attacks cause permanent damage. It could also involve a range of fully destructive options from directed energy attacks that burn a hole in a satellite using a laser or frying its delicate systems using high-power microwave emissions, to spraying its solar panels with aerosol pigment, to direct-ascent intercepts and even nuclear weapon detonations in space . Physically tampering with the satellite using another satellite is another option.
China’s presence in orbit has been dramatically expanding in recent years. The report pointed out that as of July 2026, Beijing’s intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) satellite fleet “contained more than 510 systems, having more than tripled since 2018. While many of these ISR satellites are ostensibly affiliated with commercial and civil missions, the dual-use nature of their capabilities and possibly the Chinese military-civil fusion policies means the data or imagery they collect can be used by the PLA.”
China is also expanding its capabilities to new concepts like spaceplane developments, which we highlighted in a story about their capabilities yesterday based on details from the DIA report.
In addition to possibly being placed on satellites, DEWs could also potentially be added to spaceplanes, which can operate in a less predictable fashion than satellites, even if just for experimental roles or limited capability sets.
Though thin on details, the report reiterated the reality that China’s academia has been working toward space-based weapons for years.
“Since at least 2006, government-affiliated academics have investigated aerospace engineering technologies associated with space-based kinetic weapons—a class of weapon used to attack ground, sea, or air targets from orbit,” the DIA explained. “China’s space-based kinetic weapons research included methods of reentry, separation of payload, delivery vehicles, and transfer orbits for targeting purposes.”
Much of the PLA’s ASAT doctrine “characterizes the systems as useful deterrents against external involvement in a regional conflict or as a method to manage conflict escalation,” the DIA proffered. However, should China opt to strike first, one of the first and main targets would be satellites the U.S. and allies rely on for space-based sensing and communications. As we have often explained , even reversible attacks against any of this space-based infrastructure could have major impacts on the U.S. military’s ability to effectively conduct combat operations.
The DIA report noted that to date, China’s publicly known space-based ASAT capabilities center on satellites that can approach and grab others, which we have written about in the past . In one such instance, a Chinese satellite was observed in 2022 grabbing another satellite and pulling it out of its normal geosynchronous orbit and into a “super-graveyard drift orbit.” The maneuver raised questions about the potential applications of these types of satellites designed to maneuver close to other satellites for inspection or manipulation and added to growing concerns about China’s space program overall.
The threat satellites can already pose to others was highlighted earlier this month, when a Russian satellite, Kosmos 2612, may have passed within approximately 85 feet (26 meters) of ICEYE-X36. That is a U.S.-registered satellite belonging to commercial imagery provider ICEYE that was providing imagery to Ukraine. While no contact or damage was detected, the incident raised concerns that the Russian satellite could have harmed the ICEYE purposely or even inadvertently.
You can see a time-lapse video of part of that encounter below.
Short time-lapse of part of this morning’s first pass of ICEYE-X36 (59103) and COSMOS 2612 (68762) over South America under partly cloudy skies. pic.twitter.com/t8RhwmKcV4
When it comes to discussing weapons in space capable of attacking other on-orbit objects and the effects they could impose, it should be noted that this domain inherently creates complications when it comes to attributing any form of attack , should one occur. Satellites do malfunction, sometimes with catastrophic results, but it is not always possible to determine the cause. As a result, the challenge in attributing an event could delay a response, if needed, or spark one inadvertently.
As we previously reported , in January, “ a Russian inspector satellite launched in 2014 appeared to break up unexpectedly. Sometime around the end of July, the Chinese reconnaissance satellite Yaogan 50-02 , which had only been launched some four months earlier, also broke up in orbit. On Sept. 13, a similar fate befell the U.S. Cold War-era Farrah III spy satellite , also known as USA 32. At the time of writing, no firm evidence has emerged to indicate any of these incidents were the result of hostile action rather than accidents of some kind. ”
Directed energy attacks, in particular, from one satellite against another, may be very hard to attribute as they can happen over longer distances in the vacuum of space. They would also presumably allow the attacking satellite to engage multiple targets, even in a relatively short period of time, making it one of the most attractive potential anti-satellite capabilities on orbit.
In addition to talking about Chinese space-based ASAT capabilities, the DIA report raised concerns about a wide array of threats from the PLA as well as Russia, North Korea and Iran.
The report did not address Russian space-based directed energy weapons plans. However, it did note that, like China, Russia does have ground-based laser systems already capable of affecting U.S. and allied satellites. The threat from these systems is not theoretical. They are part of an array of ASAT measures that China and Russia have used against the U.S. for years.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq-100 futures dip as Alphabet shares sell off after earnings report: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq-100 futures dip as Alphabet shares sell off after earnings report: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures dipped late Wednesday as investors digest the latest round of hyperscaler earnings.
Nasdaq-100 futures lost 1.2%. S&P 500 futures declined 0.5%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 17 points, or 0.03%.
In after-hours trading, Microsoft advanced 3% after growth in the software giant's Azure cloud infrastructure business helped it post beats on the top and bottom lines in the fiscal first quarter, per LSEG.
That contrasts sharply with Alphabet' s 9% slide after adjusted earnings per share and revenue missed expectations in the third quarter, and the company posted negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion. The company kept its full-year capital expenditures forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion.
The results come at a time when the artificial intelligence trade is in focus. AI stocks, such as the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) and the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) , have been through a rough patch for most of October, only to perk up in recent days.
Chips helped lift the broader market to a winning regular session on Wednesday, with the S&P 500 rising for a third straight day as Micron Technology jumped almost 6% and Broadcom added more than 2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite also eked out a gain, advancing 0.3%.
Earlier Wednesday, the Federal Reserve decided to hold steady on rates , leaving the central bank's benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75% and 4%. The decision to hold was widely expected as the Federal Open Market Committee issued a quarter-percentage-point hike in September.
This time, central bank policymakers pointed out that inflation "remains elevated," but also said that it was awaiting the "accumulation of more information" before it takes further steps.
The Fed's decision "can be interpreted as mildly dovish at the margin, but we think it is better viewed as an expression of patience rather than a shift away from a tightening bias," said Daniel Siluk, head of global short duration and liquidity at Janus Henderson Investors. "The door remains open to further tightening, but the Committee appears willing to wait for incoming data to validate the need for additional action."
Traders will get further insight into the economy on Thursday, when the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index report for September comes out. The PCE is a preferred inflation gauge for the Federal Reserve. The first reading of third-quarter GDP and weekly jobless claims are also due.
On the earnings front, all eyes will be on quarterly reports from Caterpillar and Eli Lilly in the morning, followed by Amazon and Intel after the market close.
Shares of ServiceNow plummeted 18% in extended hours trading Wednesday after reporting its third quarter.
The enterprise software company posted adjusted profit of $1 per share, missing the LSEG consensus expectation of $1.02 a share.
Meanwhile, subscription revenue guidance for the fourth quarter ranged from $4.245 billion to $4.255 billion, while the FactSet consensus called for $4.25 billion.
Other stocks moving in extended trading include Chipotle Mexican Grill , Fortinet and Sprouts Farmers Market .
Shares of optics maker Lumentum jumped in extended trading after Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar, that Marvell Technology is in talks to buy the company.
An acquisition could be announced as early as next week, the people told Bloomberg. These people also told Bloomberg that the details could still change and that a final agreement hasn't yet been reached.
Lumentum shares surged 11% on the report, while chipmaker Marvell lost more than 8%.
In the artificial intelligence trade, Lumentum has emerged as a winner in the infrastructure space. The company builds optical transceivers and the photonic technology underlying AI and data centers. Shares have surged almost 148% in 2026 alone. In that period, Marvell has rocketed almost 200%.
Big Tech earnings will continue Thursday with third-quarter results set to come from Amazon after the close.
The Street expects revenue of $202.22 billion, slightly above the high-end of the $197 billion-$202 billion guidance range, according to FactSet.
Investors will be keying in on growth in its cloud computing business, Amazon Web Services. Consensus estimates call for AWS revenue growth of 37.8% year over year, up from last quarter's 36.8% increase, according to FactSet.
The market will also look at whether there is growing adoption of its custom Trainium chips. Amazon stock is up 10% so far in 2026.
Futures tied to the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100 opened lower Wednesday night in New York.
S&P 500 futures fell 0.3% and Nasdaq-100 futures lost 0.8% shortly after 6 p.m. Dow futures were initially up 47 points.

articles.title_orig: A US-China-Russia Summit: What’s at Stake? - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.title_zh: A US-China-Russia Summit: What’s at Stake? - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.content_orig:
Carney backs EU-Canada associate membership amid Trump tariff threats
Canada is set to host a summit with the European Union to bolster bilateral strategic and economic ties as its relations with its southern neighbour, the United States, are in sharp decline.
The summit is scheduled for October 29 to 30 in Canada’s French-speaking city of Montreal, and is expected to focus on closer cooperation on trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, research and financial services.
In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the move.
This will be the 21st Canada-EU summit and is expected to build on the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force in 2017. It eliminates duties on up to 99 percent of all imported goods between the two sides, according to the European Council.
“In Montreal, we will take our partnership to the next level by launching our ‘Alliance for the Future’ to deepen our political, economic and institutional ties even further,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, who will be attending the summit along with Carney and von der Leyen. They are expected to issue a joint statement.
The deepening Canada-EU alignment seems fuelled by US President Donald Trump’s policies , which imposed hefty tariffs on both Canadian and European exports to the US and pushed Canada to look for ways to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Before Trump’s tariffs whipsawed relations, Canada sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to the US.
In August, trade talks between Ottawa and Washington, DC, broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
Both sides are seeking opportunities that will open more options beyond the world’s largest economy.
“The opportunity is clear. The EU brings market power, research depth, and manufacturing strength. Canada brings abundant energy, critical minerals, world-class capabilities in space, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum, and one of the world’s strongest banking systems,” Carney’s office said in a statement.
The summit will give the two sides a chance to turn these “complementary strengths into concrete benefits for our peoples,” the statement added.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a think tank in Ottawa, Canada, sees benefits and challenges.
“These fields could be beneficial for both sides, and we are likely to see specific announcements during the summit on these sectors,” she told Al Jazeera.
“The main challenge is how quickly the political momentum can turn into specific deals and projects to deliver specific economic results,” she added.
The EU describes Canada as “the only non-European country” taking part in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s 150 billion-euro ($167bn) loan programme that supports and expedites defence procurement by EU member states.
The EU concluded its agreement with Canada, allowing it to participate under SAFE, in February, and it gives Canadian firms preferential access and treatment in defence procurements financed by the SAFE Instrument.
Last month, von der Leyen proposed that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, suggesting a deeper relationship spanning trade, technology, defence and economic security.
Carney later welcomed the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.
However, the term “ associate member ” does not currently exist in EU treaties or its standard enlargement framework, according to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels-based think tank.
“The term does not actually matter; what is important is the practical deepening of the relationship and the actual results, no matter what the final term is,” Nadjibulla said.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said in her address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg last month, which Carney attended, making him the first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address.
“I do not see that as an anti-US coalition. It is rather about diversification of economic and defence partnerships and building resilience for Canada. It is a continuation of Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s policies to create opportunities. A deeper alliance with Europe is essential to this agenda,” she said.
“President Trump will likely not appreciate this, but it is about Canada having more choices in an unpredictable world,” she added.
Bob Rae, former premier of Ontario and Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025, told Al Jazeera that “President Trump does not control our policy. We have been having long and productive relations with the Europeans for hundreds of years, but Trump chose to treat Canada in a way that does not respect our sovereignty”.
He added that “engaging in conversations with the EU is perfectly normal and is not directed at the US”.
Trump has threatened the European Union with new tariffs over its proposal to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member”, suggesting the move could be considered hostile to the US.
“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, in September.
Trump dismissed the prospect of Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called the US’s northern neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

articles.title_orig: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.title_zh: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.content_orig:
At least 68 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, authorities have said.
The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene. It occurred on the Madrid to Seville line.
Transport Minister Óscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the control system at the nearby town of Urda failed and six trains were stopped. One was allowed to restart and travelled 25km before hitting a stopped train at high speed, he added, saying it was "inexplicable" how this had happened.
As well as those killed, 50 people were also injured, the minister said.
Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFE reported .
The local Castilla-La Mancha government confirmed at least 68 people had died, higher than another high-speed crash in southern Spain that killed 45 people in January.
Emiliano García-Page, the president of the region, said 24 people had died on a train operated by rail company Renfe, with the rest killed on a train operated by Iryo.
More than 500 passengers were on board the two trains, newspaper El País said.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by the Renfe train, saying the cause was "still unknown".
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a post on X that he was "shocked" by the accident.
"If there has been any negligence, it will come to light," he later said at a press conference.
"If there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness. It is clear that we have experienced two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail within the same year."
Sanchez's political future will be tested in a snap election on Nov. 29, which he called following widespread unrest over Spain's housing crisis.
Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party — which is expected to make gains when Spain goes to the polls — pointed the finger at Sanchez's government over the train accident on Wednesday.
"Tragedy again. Rage again over the neglect, the ruin, and the betrayal suffered by the Spanish people," he said in a post on X.
— CNBC's Charlotte Reed contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Fed meeting recap: Warsh says central bank will host fewer rate-setting meetings in future years
articles.title_zh: Fed meeting recap: Warsh says central bank will host fewer rate-setting meetings in future years
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve held steady on rates at the conclusion of its October meeting, maintaining its target range of 3.75% to 4%.
Two members of the Federal Open Market Committee dissented from the decision: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack were in favor of raising rates by a quarter percentage point.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced that the central bank will reduce the number of rate-setting meetings starting in 2027, noting that while eight meetings per year is "the right number" for the FOMC, one of them will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy starting in 2027. The remainder will be policy-setting meetings.
In 2028, the Fed will plan to host two meetings focused on strategy discussions and the remaining six will be centered on policy setting, Warsh said.
Inflation remains hot, the economy is strong — and that means the Federal Reserve should be lifting rates, according to bond investor Jeffrey Gundlach.
"I think the Fed should be raising interest rates, based upon the 2-year Treasury being at 4 and three-quarters percent, and now the yield curve in the wake of this news conference is steepening again," Gundlach, CEO and Chief Investment Officer of DoubleLine Capital, said on CNBC's "Closing Bell" after Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh wrapped up his news conference.
The 2-year Treasury yield , which is sensitive to Fed policy, was last trading at 4.714%.
At the Fed's press conference, which came after central bank policymakers opted to hold rates steady at a range of 3.75% and 4%, Warsh highlighted the strength of the economy.
"Broadly, what I heard in the room the last couple of days is consistent with my own views, which is the economy is strong," the central bank leader said.
Gundlach noted that it's not clear why the Fed is holding steady on rates.
"What are you waiting for? You just upgraded the economy right here," he said, referring to Warsh's comments at the press conference.
Read more from CNBC's Davis Giangiulio on Gundlach's comments here.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh repeated again in his Wednesday press conference that he does not favor the Federal Reserve signaling the future path of interest rates and monetary policy in a process known colloquially as "forward guidance."
"I don't believe in forward guidance, absent exigent circumstances, absent a crisis," Warsh told reporter after the Fed kept its benchmark fed funds rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4%.
"I have to give that caveat because in the darkest days of the 2008 financial crisis, in part using some literature and thinking from a very recent Nobel Prize winner, that kind of forward guidance is actually quite helpful. But in normal, ordinary times, especially times where the underlying deal economy is this strong, I don't believe in it. I don't favor it."
— Scott Schnipper, Fred Imbert
Warsh said higher interest rates have had an effect on the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out.
"Interest rates have had an effect," Warsh said. "You see market participants that are discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make. You've seen credit spreads for certain assets widen out, gap out. For others, you've seen some tightening in financial conditions, but not significantly.
"I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of the economy," he added.
Warsh said the capital expenditure story is "not just strong, but it is broadening." He said it's "much harder" to argue that economic strength is driven by a a small group of sectors today than it was several quarters prior.
The public will be hearing less from the Federal Reserve when it comes to interest rate decisions.
Warsh announced Wednesday that the central bank will alter its meeting schedule in coming years, seemingly part of his plans to pare back the impact that he and his colleagues have on financial markets.
Under the details Warsh revealed, the Federal Open Market Committee will still meet eight times a year.
However, unlike the current system in which the panel votes on where it will set its benchmark interest rate, one of those meetings in 2027 will focus solely on strategy. In 2028, there will be two strategy sessions.
"We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC," Warsh said, but noted the committee doesn't need to vote at each one.
"What's the reasoning behind this change? To me, it's quite straightforward," he added. "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals.
"But it's equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point."
Warsh has emphasized the importance of "regime change" at the Fed, a process that has entailed the establishment of multiple task forces aimed at looking at how the central bank operates. One such task force will address communication issues.
The meeting change appears to be a first step in the process of changing the Fed's approach.
"I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail. It's an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations, and ultimately the wisdom of our decisions," he said. "It's yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track."
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said politics did not influence Wednesday's decision to maintain rates.
"I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics. I didn't hear a reference to politics, elections, what's happening in the next week or so," Warsh said. Midterm elections are scheduled for Nov. 3.
"Didn't hear anything about it, and I don't believe it had any role in the decision, not just for me, but my colleagues around the room," he said.
At these policy meetings that will specifically focus on broad strategy, Warsh said he doesn't anticipate that the Fed will make a rate decision or release a statement.
He then said "it's not obvious yet" what the Fed would share following these meetings.
"There's more news to come on that," Warsh said. "The decision on the new format for the meetings is relatively new."
Warsh said there was a "robust discussion" on how to handle these meetings over a few gatherings.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said economic growth has been positive after the agency maintained rates at its October meeting, keeping rates at a range between 3.75% and 4%.
"Economic growth has strengthened. The GDP increase in the first half of this year was revised up from an earlier estimate of 1.8 percent up to 2.4 percent, and the third quarter appears to have brought an even more rapid advance," Warsh said.
Warsh said the Fed's discussion over recent days "focused mainly on the price stability side of our remit."
He said the full employment side of its dual mandate has been "quite positive," citing a decreasing jobless rate compared with a year ago. Warsh also noted that the unemployment insurance claims volume, when looking at a four-week average, is at "the lowest level in generations."
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said the central bank will cut back on the number of meetings where members vote on rates. Said Warsh: "We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC, but in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated. The rest will be regular FOMC policy setting meetings, and I expect that in 2028 we'll have two meetings dedicated discussions of strategy and six for setting policy."
Later Warsh added that he doesn't "anticipate" making a policy decision during these strategy meetings.

articles.title_orig: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
articles.title_zh: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has emerged as the critical sticking point between the U.S. and China. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition.
Trump said while campaigning for president that tariffs would form the crux of the bilateral relationship. The U.S. and China, the world’s two largest economies, have been engaged in a trade war during both of Trump’s terms.
Speaking Sept. 13 in Ireland, Trump said the U.S. is leading China in AI.
“We’re leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said.
During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“And it’s to me an honor. We’ve had a fantastic relationship. We’ve gotten along. When they were difficulties, we worked it out,” Trump said.
Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September for a state visit. He touted what he called “the tremendous strides” he and Xi had already made on national security, trade and technology.
At the summit, the U.S. and China agreed to extend a trade truce until January. No agreement was reached on implementing safeguards for AI.
Trump and Xi are set to meet again in China next month.

articles.title_orig: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state’s total ban on gambling
articles.title_zh: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state’s total ban on gambling
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.
Utah, which prohibits gambling, sued Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.
“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).
The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” the commission said yesterday . “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.”
If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertise availability in all US states via a mix of products , including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC.
The Utah attorney general’s office declined to comment today on the CFTC lawsuit. The CFTC previously filed lawsuits against Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. The federal agency also filed briefs supporting Kalshi in appeals court cases.
“Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets. As I’ve said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that’s exactly what we’ll do.”
The US Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) gives the CFTC authority to regulate swaps. The key legal questions being grappled with by courts throughout the US are whether event contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps, and whether the CFTC jurisdiction over swaps preempts states from applying their gambling laws.
The CFTC is suing Utah in the same US district court that previously ruled in Utah’s favor. Kalshi sued Utah in February in an attempt to stop the state from bringing an enforcement action against the prediction market.
In August, US District Judge Robert Shelby granted Utah’s motion for summary judgment and denied Kalshi’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Shelby wrote , “[T]he court concludes the federal law relied upon by Kalshi does not preempt Utah’s ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws.”
Shelby determined the text of US law makes it clear that state regulation is not forbidden. US law states that CFTC jurisdiction does not “supersede or limit the jurisdiction conferred on courts of the United States or any State,” and “explicitly provides for State regulation of its gaming laws in all but a few specified cases,” he wrote.
“Congress is aware that some States permit gambling while others do not, and the CEA explicitly provides for State jurisdiction,” Shelby wrote.
Kalshi is now appealing its loss to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit but was unable to obtain an injunction preventing enforcement of the state gambling ban while that litigation continues. On September 8, Tenth Circuit judges denied Kalshi’s emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal. Utah filed its lawsuit seeking a shutdown of Kalshi about six weeks later.
The CFTC lawsuit against Utah makes arguments similar to the ones already rejected by the district court, although some other courts have ruled otherwise.
“Utah is not the first State that has attempted to invade the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over swaps,” the CFTC lawsuit said. “Already, several federal courts—including the Third Circuit—have swiftly responded by issuing or affirming temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions barring the States from enforcing their gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges that offer sports-related or other event contracts.”
The Third Circuit appeals court ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. But Kalshi lost similar cases in the Sixth Circuit and Ninth Circuit in rulings that went in favor of Ohio, Tennessee, and Nevada.
Because circuit appeals courts are divided on the issue, it is likely that the Supreme Court will take up the case and determine whether states can apply their gambling laws to prediction markets. New Jersey petitioned the Supreme Court to resolve the circuit split, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s petition.

articles.content_orig:

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk is a 'real genius', Putin says after satellite talks with SpaceX boss
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk is a 'real genius', Putin says after satellite talks with SpaceX boss
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.
The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.
"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."
Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".
"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.
Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.
The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".
"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.
Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.
US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.
Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.
Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".
Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.
The billionaire, and off and on again trillionaire, has been one of the biggest political allies and financiers of Trump and other Republican US politicians.

articles.title_orig: AI Is Finding a Flood of Bugs, and Silicon Valley Is Rushing to Fix Them
articles.title_zh: AI Is Finding a Flood of Bugs, and Silicon Valley Is Rushing to Fix Them
articles.content_orig:
Last week, we published a report describing two major vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Since then, alongside much of the security industry, the Wiz Research team has been monitoring for related activity in the wild and reviewing publicly available exploit code. So far, we have observed a limited number of exploitation attempts in our telemetry and have not identified a publicly available proof of concept (PoC) demonstrating complete, general end-to-end exploitation against an arbitrary target. Some partners have, however, privately disclosed to us exploits that work against a variety of targets and we continue to experiment internally. Videos demonstrating our successful exploitations are available at php2shell.com .
This post summarizes what we have observed in terms of remediation efforts and exploitation attempts across real world environments and in our own honeypot data to date and shares findings from our ongoing investigation into these activities.
We will continue monitoring developments and update this post as new evidence emerges.
Following PHP2Shell’s public disclosure on October 21, 2026, Wiz telemetry has recorded an approximate 67% decrease in the daily number of distinct Internet-exposed machines vulnerable to PHP2Shell over the past few days. Separately, among vulnerable Internet-exposed machines, the proportion running PHP version 7.3 or earlier fell from 8.3% to 5.7% over a period of five days. This measures the share of the observed population running older versions that did not receive official backports.
During this period, the number of significantly affected organizations - defined here as those with at least one exposed and vulnerable instance - fell by approximately 47.9% (see graph below). For reference, our data shows that PHP itself is in use by 65% of organizations in our dataset.
Together, these observations are consistent with organizations collectively reducing their exposure through a combination of patching, upgrading, retiring affected machines and restricting internet access (note that this data shows the overall trend, but does not establish the relative contribution of each remediation strategy; scan coverage and size of observed population can also affect the overall reported numbers over time).
We have so far observed the following types of activities in this context:
Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism, with techniques matching those of public PoCs .
PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities that instead relied on session poisoning and a separate local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability in the application.
We observed two variants of an open source exploit kit targeting PHP-based software. Neither completed the exploit chain in the attempts we captured. The older variant encountered request-size limits or failed to produce the expected memory-exhaustion condition. The newer variant did consistently exhaust PHP’s memory, but failed to obtain the memory addresses needed to continue.
The first request to our PHP-CGI honeypot came from 3.37.227[.]134 . It matched the kit’s older chain, found under archive/legacy-8m/exploit.py and its accompanying stage scripts. The first full exploit stage used a multipart body containing 1,005 parts, including a field named big filled with approximately 12 MB of padding:
According to the kit’s notes, this stage attempts to exhaust memory during a session reset, leaving the session state available for a later request.
On our honeypot, it failed before reaching that code. The declared request size exceeded the configured 8 MB post_max_size limit, so PHP skipped processing the multipart body and logged:
The author has since moved this chain into the kit’s archive directory.
In a later attempt, 103.151.172[.]95 sent a longer sequence from the legacy chain. It included stalled connections intended to occupy other Apache workers.
When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each. These requests didn’t trigger the memory exhaustion flow required. So there is no evidence that this attempt reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition.
Most IP addresses we captured used the newer chain, built from pure/mk_a1.py and pure/mk_leak_b.py . We observed this variant in multiple attempts.
This variant progressed further: its first stage consistently caused PHP to exhaust its memory. The following stage, which attempts to leak process memory, failed in every run we captured.
The server logged a fatal error indicating that PHP reached its limit, for example:
The chain depends on consecutive exploit requests reaching the same Apache child process. To increase the chances of that happening, the kit attempts to occupy the other workers with incomplete requests. Each connection declares a large body, sends a single byte and stalls:
One address, 178.249.214[.]6 , opened 399 of these connections alongside 400 GET requests before sending the exploit stages. The address is a VPN exit node, which limits what we can infer about the source.
A1 is a chunked multipart request containing a null-byte session ID, 860 empty file parts with long, deeply nested array names and several groups of padding fields:
The request is designed to exhaust memory during session handling at a point that can leave the session ID pointing to freed memory.
Every A1 request we captured returned HTTP 500, accompanied by a PHP error matching:
This confirms that A1 reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition on our honeypot. It does not, by itself, confirm that the stale session state needed by the next stage was preserved.
B1 followed roughly a second later. It sent another chunked multipart request containing PHPSESSID=a , PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS=k0 and two large padding fields.
If this request reaches the same worker before PHP resets the stale session state, PHP can write reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The kit then extracts heap and libphp addresses from that cookie to prepare the final exploit stage.
We observed no such leak. In all but one run, the connection closed without a response. The remaining run returned a normal 32-character session cookie. None of the sources sent the final exploit stage.
The failed leaks highlight a broader challenge: building a generalized exploit that works reliably across PHP versions and deployment configurations is difficult. The kit’s B1 layout was calculated for the official php:8.4.26-apache image with a 128 MB memory limit. Other instances like our Roundcube honeypot ran the same PHP version from a different build, with additional extensions and a 64 MB memory limit. These differences can affect heap layout and memory reuse, potentially preventing the leak from working as expected.
Reliable worker pinning adds another challenge. Consecutive exploit requests must reach the same Apache child process while the required session state persists. Request timeouts, network latency and worker availability can disrupt this sequence. In our own testing, request timeouts combined with network latency were enough to prevent the chain from completing over an internet connection.
So far, we have not identified a publicly available, generalized solution for either worker pinning or information leaking across different deployments. Simply copying public PoCs and running them at scale does not address the work needed to turn a configuration-specific exploit into a reliable operational kit. We expect these barriers to diminish over time: some threat actors have the expertise needed to adapt the chain and build more robust tooling.
We also saw failed exploitation attempts from 15.204.59[.]70 and 162.35.99[.]94 , but these scanners did successfully exploit Adel Karimi's honeypot , which was a likely contributing factor to CISA’s decision to include PHP2Shell in their KEV list .

articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, Oct. 28, 2026: Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq end higher after Fed holds rates steady; Microsoft and Alphabet results loom; SK Hynix stock soars
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 rose on Wednesday as investors reacted to the Federal Reserve's latest interest rate decision and awaited earnings reports from mega-cap technology companies.
The broad market index gained 0.28% to end at 7,743.98, while the Nasdaq Composite added 0.27% to close at 26,549.85. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 97.53 points, or 0.19%, to 52,475.10. It was the third straight winning day for the S&P 500, Nasdaq and the Dow.
The Fed kept interest rates steady at a target rate range of 3.75% to 4%. Policymakers had raised rates by a quarter percentage point at their September meeting, marking its first hike since 2023.
Traders had widely anticipated the move. Heading into Wednesday's meeting, fed funds futures trading priced in a nearly 93% chance that the central bank would maintain the current interest rate, per CME's FedWatch tool .
Chairman Kevin Warsh said during a press conference following the decision that the central bank remained focused on "price stability" despite the pause and that the employment picture has been "quite positive."
"Nothing from today rules out another 25 bp hike before year-end," said Jeff Schulze, head investment strategist at Franklin Templeton Institute. "The key question for markets is the pace of tightening, and the Committee seems content to unwind last year's cuts at a measured pace which historically has been more favorable for risk assets."
Shares of software company Oracle jumped nearly 11% after it provided a fiscal 2030 revenue outlook of $225 billion , which implies annual growth of 35%. The company also said it would restrict additional fundraising between fiscal 2027 and 2030 to $20 billion.
Chipmakers also moved higher Wednesday, buoyed by SK Hynix posting record quarterly profit — a development that sent U.S. shares of the South Korean chipmaker up 13%. Micron Technology was up  almost 6%, while Arm Holdings advanced 4%. Marvell Technology moved up 3%, and Advanced Micro Devices increased 3%.
Investors' attention will remain on the artificial intelligence trade after the bell, as "Magnificent Seven" giants Alphabet and Microsoft are set to report their latest quarterly results. The former was last seen up more than 1%, while the latter was down marginally on the day.
Tech stocks, particularly those with exposure to the AI buildout, have struggled in recent weeks amid questions over the technology's financing .
"The near-term cycle remains incredibly healthy," said Bill Northey, investment director at U.S. Bank Asset Management Group. "It's really about can it remain durable for many years, and what are the returns to those who are investing significantly today. Will it be universally a profitable endeavor, or will there start to be some winners and losers that emerge there, and we tend to think that it leans towards the latter."
The three leading U.S. indexes finished in the green on Wednesday.
The S&P 500 added 0.28% to 7,743.98, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.27% to close at 26,549.85. The Dow Jones Industrial Average moved up 97.53 points, or 0.19%, to 52,475.10.
Oracle shares jumped 12% on Wednesday after the software company issued a revenue forecast of $225 billion for fiscal 2030, implying 35% average annual growth, and said it will limit additional fundraising over that stretch to $20 billion. Read more .
Regional bank stocks were under pressure on Wednesday afternoon, as the State Street SPDR S&P Regional Banking ETF (KRE) traded down more than 1%.
The fund was on pace for its worst day since Oct. 7, when it fell 1.68%.
Major regional banks such as Truist Financial , M&T Bank and Huntington Bancshares were also trading near session lows.
— Gina Francolla and Sean Conlon
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep benchmark interest rates on hold despite mounting evidence that price pressures are proving more nettlesome than policymakers had hoped.
"Inflation remains elevated," the post-meeting statement said. "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."
SK Hynix 's shareholder returns are on track to outpace expectations, and that could boost its stock, according to UBS.
The investment firm now expects shareholder returns to equal up to 60% of the semiconductor firm's expected free cash flow return in 2027, per its analysts' new note.
"[The stock's] current share price already discounts a marked downcycle scenario for '28," analyst Nicolas Gaudois said Wednesday in a note to clients. "Going forward, we reset our expectation up to 60% of [free cash flow] return 2027E onwards."
Gaudois added that shareholder returns are the "key positive catalyst" for SK Hynix.
Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading:
Crude oil prices traded around session highs on Wednesday, lifting Treasury yields.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures advanced 2.8% to $102.72 per barrel, while global benchmark Brent crude futures rose about 1.6% to $115.67 a barrel.
U.S. Treasury yields were higher following the move, with the 10-year Treasury note yield last up more than 3 basis points at 5.024%. The 30-year Treasury bond yield was up more than 2 basis points at 5.326%.
Stifel has downgraded Whirlpool Corporation to sell from hold.
"We contend WHR is losing market share in the key U.S. market. Losses could potentially accelerate given announced pricing to offset inflation (resin, steel), competitor incentives, limited appliance brand loyalty, and weaker WHR brand demographics," wrote analyst W. Andrew Carter in a Tuesday note.
Stifel also reduced its target price for the home appliance company to $20 from $30, implying a 27.1% downside from Tuesday's close. The firm also lowered its FY28 EBITDA to $815 million from $872 million for the company. Challenges Whirlpool Corporation outlined in the third-quarter are "likely to accelerate" Carter added.
The stock fell more than 2% in late morning trading on Wednesday.
Visa reported fiscal fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of $3.48 per share, up 17% from a year earlier.
Net revenue for the company increased 13% to $12.1 billion, while GAAP net income rose 18% to $6 billion. Non-GAAP operating margin in the fourth quarter came in at 66.6%, slightly below the FactSet consensus estimate of 66.7%. Adjusted earnings and revenue in the period surpassed estimates.
Payments volume for Visa grew 9%, cross-border volume advanced 14% and processed transactions increased 10%, reflecting resilient consumer spending and travel activity.
For the full year, Visa generated record revenue of $45.9 billion, up 15%. The company also raised its quarterly dividend by 16% to 78 cents per share.
Shares were trading around the flatline in morning trading.
The S&P 500 rose on Wednesday morning.
The broad market index traded up 0.2% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline.
Wendy's surged as much as 16% in the premarket Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that Nelson Peltz's Trian Management has offered to pay $1.4 billion to take the fast food chain private.
The activist firm, a long time shareholder in Wendy's, is leading the deal with other partners including investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.
U.S. stocks were active before Wednesday's opening bell as earnings and acquisition news drove sharp moves across several stocks.
Ultralife surged after agreeing to a $320 million acquisition by EnerSys, while SK hynix climbed on record AI-memory earnings. Robinhood fell as weaker crypto activity weighed on its quarterly results, and Enphase Energy dropped following declining revenue and continued pressure in residential solar.

articles.title_orig: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
articles.title_zh: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wendy's ( WEN ) may be cooking up burgers for a billionaire soon.
Longtime Wendy's investor and former chairman Nelson Peltz of Trian Partners has reportedly offered $1.4 billion to buy the struggling fast food giant , according to an SEC filing.
Wendy's shares rose 15% in early trading. The company's market cap was $1.17 billion prior to the deal.
A Wendy's spokesperson didn't return a request for comment. A spokesperson for Trian Partners didn't return a request for comment.
Billionaire Peltz — while familiar with the operations — would essentially be buying a dumpster fire.
After nearly two years of struggles competing with the likes of behemoths McDonald's ( MCD ) and Yum! Brands' ( YUM ) Taco Bell, plus upstarts such as Shake Shack ( SHAK ), Wendy's is on the cusp of a large number of restaurant closures.
"With one of its largest franchisees filing bankruptcy in September (although contested by WEN given prior termination of franchise agreement), we think investors likely expect closures to tick higher than expected, but we admit visibility on our side remains somewhat limited and there could still be a range of outcomes," veteran restaurant analyst Andy Barish warned in a recent note.
"That said," he added, "given our view that there are likely additional franchise operators in the system facing challenges with leveraged balance sheets, higher interest rates and profitability pressures from higher beef, labor & build costs (like many others in QSR), we think it is prudent to moderate our development estimates and bake in more potential closures over the next 6-12 months, as the company works to strengthen its system."
Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchise operators, with more than 300 locations, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September following severe margin pressures and an escalating dispute with corporate headquarters. The company reportedly initiated plans to shutter at least 41 locations. Reports emerged this week that it could close up to 60.
The high-profile bankruptcy only added grease to the smoldering fire that is the Wendy's restaurant base.
Franchisees had already been closing their locations and heading for the hills.
Buried inside Wendy's brutal second quarter earnings call was a mention that 289 locations closed in the US during the first half of the year.
There are about 5,700 Wendy's in the US, and Barish estimated the Wendy's US store base will be around 5,600 by the end of 2027.
The decision on how many more locations will be closed falls on new CEO Bob Wright, who hasn't hidden his view that Wendy's needs to focus on more profitable locations.
Wright officially took over as CEO on May 21, adding to the yawning list of executive turnover at the fast food chain over the past two years. He is a seasoned fast food exec who spent the previous five years fixing Potbelly as CEO. Wright's appointment marked a return to Wendy's, where he previously served in several senior leadership roles, including COO.
Wright has his work cut out for him in saving Wendy's beyond tightening up the store base count.
Wendy's has posted six straight quarters of same-store sales declines, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace analysis.

articles.title_orig: John Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
articles.title_zh: John Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
articles.content_orig:
Chancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a £4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defence Investment Plan.
The reductions come on top of the 1% cuts departments were asked to make earlier this year in order to pay for the initial £10.3bn of the plan's overall £15bn price tag.
The plan boosted defence spending; however the chancellor continues to come under pressure to explain how he will meet a further target of spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the chancellor of only offering "a plan to have a plan" adding:  "I bet [Vladimir] Putin's really scared now."
Setting out his Budget, Healey hinted that meeting that goal would require further cuts, telling MPs it would involve "looking hard at public spending".
He said he would set out how the UK would reach the 3% target by 2030, as well as 3.5% of GDP by 2035, at next year's spending review.
Government departments have yet to decide what will be cut from their capital budgets.
Capital budgets are focused on long-term investments, rather than day-to-day spending. For example, earlier this year, when departments had to make capital budget cuts to fund the initial defence spending rise, a number of major road improvement schemes were scrapped .
Badenoch criticised Healey for not using his Budget to explain how he would boost defence funding to 3%.
"He is the man who is making our country less safe. He has failed his own test. This is on him, and no one will ever forget," she said.
The Conservatives have previously urged the government to pay for defence by making cuts to the welfare budget.
Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the UK was on "a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato Allies in The Hague - to ensure we're all investing what's needed to remain ready & able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security".
Chair of the Commons defence committee - and Labour MP - Tan Dhesi said "some of the key decisions on defence spending have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review".
He added: "There is a cost to inaction. Investment in our nation's defence and security cannot be kicked into the long grass."
Former Nato secretary general Lord Robertson told the BBC the Budget was "pretty good news for defence generally" but warned there would be "battles ahead with the spending departments" to reach the 3% target.
Earlier this year, Healey resigned as defence secretary, accusing the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer of not providing enough money to keep the UK safe.
In a scathing resignation letter, he specifically emphasised his belief in the importance of reaching a 3% target by 2030.
Now chancellor, Healey told the House of Commons on Wednesday: "At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our Nato commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030.
"And today, I am getting work under way to get there in a fiscally sustainable way."
In addition to looking at public spending, Healey said he also wanted to use "more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies".
The chancellor said this would include:
The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the UK government's target to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 will cost £35bn.
Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Increasing investment in defence companies may contribute to the target but it is unclear how much this will lead to an increase in UK defence capabilities.
"There is much further to go to get to 3% of GDP on defence and it is hard to believe that this government will want to get there without topping up spending totals."
In his Budget speech, Healey also announced £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine, in the form of loans and export guarantees.
The funding includes £5.5bn of loans through World Bank guarantees and a grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association's crisis facility.
A further £3bn will be made available to Ukraine through loans facilitated by UK Export Finance, a government export credit agency.
Healey told the House of Commons that the week had started with Russia launching a "brutal ballistic missile attack" and that the extra money would send "a clear message to Moscow".
He said that when he told the Ukrainian leader about the additional support in a phone call, President Volodymyr Zelensky had said: "You've made my day."
Later on social media, Zelensky welcomed the money, saying: "Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realising that it must end this war of its own making."
The money comes on top of the UK's pledge to provide Ukraine with £3bn of military support until at least 2030-31.

articles.content_orig:
Qatar is awaiting a response from Tehran to a new proposal that could see Iran take a limited step on its nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief and potentially the release of frozen funds, two regional diplomats told The Jerusalem Post . The response could come as early as Thursday.
The measure under consideration would involve allowing inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to return to Iran’s nuclear sites in return for sanctions relief.
On Tuesday, IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi briefed members of the UN Security Council, saying that only the return of inspectors to the ground could provide an accurate picture of the current state of Iran’s nuclear program.
"I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions and to give the IAEA the information and access the agency requires, so that it can verify all relevant facilities and material, as is Iran's legal obligation," Grossi said.
The proposal comes amid continued difficulties in negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Iran has demanded that the US lift its blockade and provide some sanctions relief before discussions on its nuclear program can begin. The Trump administration, however, has insisted that Iran take an initial step on the nuclear issue from the outset of any agreement.
The return of IAEA inspectors could offer a potential starting point for bridging the gap between the two sides, while allowing the international community to assess the status of Iran’s nuclear activities.
Senior officials from the mediating countries told Iranian officials that this deal might be "the last chance before President Trump might decide to launch a military operation against Iran ".
“As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait.
"The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections", Anna Kelly, White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary, told the Jerusalem Post. The midterms will be held next Tuesday. Kelly also added that “As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait".

articles.title_orig: Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of Starlink
articles.title_zh: Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of Starlink
articles.content_orig:
Russia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack Ukraine
Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.
The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.
“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”
The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US and Ukraine earlier this month.
A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.
Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.
Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.
“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and ​to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.
Starlink does not work in Russia and its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.
Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.
Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.
“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.
after newsletter promotion
Earlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.
The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.
John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”
The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.
Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.
Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.

articles.title_orig: Residents on the doomed Villa Vie Odyssey cruise describe the first 24 hours after being kicked off in Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Residents on the doomed Villa Vie Odyssey cruise describe the first 24 hours after being kicked off in Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
Passengers on a live-aboard round-the-world cruise say they were abruptly asked to leave the ship and given only hours to disembark.
Villa Vie Residences, which operates the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey , said on Tuesday it had halted operations due to surging fuel costs.
The ship was docked at the port of Sihanoukville in Cambodia when the announcement was made, with passengers saying they were given only eight hours to disembark.
"On October 27, 2026, we received notice from the CEO at around 6 a.m. that all residents had to disembark by 2 p.m. that day," passengers Lanette Canen and John Bodin told Business Insider by email.
Canen and Bodin have been on the Odyssey since it first set sail in September 2024 and run a YouTube channel called Living Life on a Cruise about their experiences on board.
"We knew leaving was a possibility, but the eight-hour notice still surprised us," they said.
The couple shared a video on their YouTube channel that appears to show the moment a staff member announced that passengers must leave the ship.
"Unfortunately, they were unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations," a male voice says in the video.
A notice on the Villa Vie Residences website says the company is working with residents to arrange temporary living arrangements and that it is evaluating restructuring options over the next 60 days.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Villa Vie Residences did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CEO Kathy Villalba and executive chairman Mikael Petterson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on Tuesday that the surging cost of fuel since the beginning of the Iran war had made operating the cruise liner increasingly difficult.
The company said its monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which had previously averaged about $1,800, had risen as much as 344% in parts of Asia, to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000.
"Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port," Villa Vie Residences said.
"Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
On August 1, Villalba, the CEO, sent residents a message titled "Urgent operational update" on an internal messaging platform. In the message, she referenced a "fuel contribution" that had been previously requested of residents. Business Insider has viewed a screenshot of the message.
"When the fuel contribution was requested several months ago, participation was not universal," she wrote in the message. "The contributions received helped some, but they covered only part of the extraordinary increase in fuel costs."
Villalba wrote that the "cash-flow" challenge had continued, and the Odyssey needed 650 metric tons of fuel, adding that fuel prices had almost doubled.
"We have now reached a critical point. The lack of full participation, combined with the unprecedented increase in fuel costs, means we must make immediate and creative operational decisions to preserve the voyage," her message said.
It continued, "We are asking every Resident who did not previously contribute to please do so now. We are also asking those who are able to provide additional support to consider helping with this immediate fuel requirement."
Villalba described the financial need as "real, immediate, and necessary to keep Odyssey moving." It went on, "This is a moment when preserving our home and continuing the voyage requires support beyond contractual minimums from those who are able to provide it."
Among the passengers asked to disembark on Tuesday with only a few hours' notice was Barbara Fiegel, 62, who has lived with her partner aboard the ship since December 2024.
"Everybody's just shocked, everybody's just saddened by this whole issue," she said. "We're still processing, trying to debate what we're going to do."
Fiegel said she and her partner booked a hotel room in Cambodia, then returned to the ship Tuesday evening and Wednesday afternoon to empty their safe and pack their belongings. "Today, as we approached, as we went back on the shuttle back to the ship, I couldn't stop crying," she said.
They plan to return on Thursday to collect their remaining items. Fiegel described the atmosphere on the Odyssey as a “ghost town.”
Joel Greiff, 57, moved aboard the ship at the start of the month. “I was planning to live on the ship for 10, 20, or 73 years,” he said. “I don’t think that will be happening.”
When residents were told to disembark, Greiff emptied his cabin. “I personally grabbed everything,” he said.
He said he would like to return if Villa Vie Residences resumes operations. If not, he is planning to move to Thailand. In the meantime, he has rented an apartment in Cambodia for a month.
Greiff said he plans to return to the Odyssey on Thursday to assist other residents and “help with their luggage, help them find a place, and just start getting them and all their stuff off the ship.”
Have you spent any time on the Villa Vie Odyssey as a cabin owner, renter, or staff member? If you have a story to share, get in touch with this reporter: jzitser@businessinsider.com .

articles.title_orig: Apple reveals pricing for Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM
articles.title_zh: Apple reveals pricing for Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM
articles.content_orig:
When Apple announced the new M5 Max and M5 Ultra configurations of the Mac Studio in August, it said a configuration with 512GB of RAM would be available in October. Today, the company officially revealed the pricing of that option.
If you head to the Mac Studio configurator on Apple’s website, you’ll see the new 512GB upgrade option. As previously announced, the 512GB option is only available with the top-tier M5 Ultra chip that has a 36-core CPU and 80‑core GPU.
It’s a $15,500 upgrade over the base configuration of that processor, which has 96GB of unified memory.
To put it another way: you’ll pay $22,299 for the Mac Studio with the top-tier M5 Ultra, 512GB of unified memory, and 1TB of storage. You can spec it up all the way to 16TB of storage, which brings the total price to $29,799.00.
If you order a Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, it’ll arrive in late November to early December.
