articles.title_orig: Apple Releases Redesigned Mac Chargers and 'World Travel Adapter Kit'
articles.title_zh: Apple Releases Redesigned Mac Chargers and 'World Travel Adapter Kit'
articles.content_orig:
Apple today began selling updated versions of its 70W Power Adapter , 140W Power Adapter , and Power Adapter Extension Cable , all with a new "AC Connector 2."
The updated power adapters and extension cable are available on Apple's online store in the U.S. and many other countries around the world.
Apple also released an updated version of its World Travel Adapter Kit that had disappeared from its online store in 2025, with U.S. pricing set at $39. Each of the international AC plugs included in the box now have the AC Connector 2 too.
Apple's power adapters have a removable plug, and the World Travel Adapter Kit contains various plug types for international travel:
The kit includes five interchangeable AC plugs: Type A: North America, Japan Type C: Continental Europe, Brazil Type D: India Type G: United Kingdom, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Singapore Type I: Australia, New Zealand
In a new support document , Apple said its updated power adapters, extension cable, and plugs use the AC Connector 2 with a pill-shaped design to comply with "updated regulations." Apple's previous "AC Connector 1" has a notched design.
Apple began rolling out the AC Connector 2 in a few countries earlier this year, leading to some customers complaining about compatibility issues with Apple's older extension cables and World Travel Adapter Kit. Apple has now solved that problem by releasing these updated versions of the accessories with the AC Connector 2.

articles.title_orig: Lula’s Election Win in Brazil Is a Relief for China - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: Lula’s Election Win in Brazil Is a Relief for China - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a signing ceremony at the Great Hall of the People, Beijing, May 13, 2025.
On October 4, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva finished the first round of Brazil’s presidential election behind his main rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro and an open ally of U.S. President Donald Trump. Flavio Bolsonaro had taken 47 percent of valid votes against Lula’s 45 percent. Because no one topped 50 percent of votes, however, the race went to a second-round runoff.
The first post-election poll gave Bolsonaro a six-point lead in the head-to-head contest. Three weeks later, Lula won with 51.76 percent , a margin of roughly 4.3 million ballots, securing an unprecedented fourth term. His victory came after intense popular demonstrations in leading cities such as Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Belo Horizonte, as well as a new social media strategy boosted by political allies.
Lula’s comeback matters well beyond Brasília. Since late 2025, Latin America has seen a regional shift toward right-wing regimes. Bolivia, Chile, Honduras, Costa Rica, Colombia, and Peru all elected conservative governments, most of them endorsed by Washington.
Brazil was meant to be the crowning piece of Trump’s foreign policy, seeing as it is the largest market in the region and one of the only ones who did not agree on Trump’s Shield for the Americas initiative . Instead, Brazil has opted for a pragmatic foreign economic policy, trying to negotiate with both China and the United States.
The Donroe Doctrine Meets Its Limits
Washington’s strategy has been referred to as the “Donroe Doctrine,” claiming the United States’ right to assert its interests in the region in security terms. In practice that has meant rewarding ideological allies and treating Chinese influence as a central opposing force.
A series of electoral victories seemed to confirm the effectiveness of Trump’s approach to the region. Rodrigo Paz ended two decades of Movimiento al Socialismo (MAS) rule in Bolivia in October 2025. José Antonio Kast won Chile in December. Nasry Asfura took office in Honduras after Trump threatened to cut aid if he lost. In June 2026, Colombia elected the Trump-endorsed outsider Abelardo de la Espriella , and Keiko Fujimori finally won Peru on her fourth attempt. Moreover, Argentina’s right-wing President Javier Milei continues to be an ally.
Tensions between Brazil and the United States have been accumulating in Trump’s second term. In July 2025, the U.S. president imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on Brazilian goods over the prosecution and later incarceration of Jair Bolsonaro and sanctioned the Supreme Court judge overseeing the case.
On May 26, 2026, Trump received Flavio in the Oval Office, and on June 2, a day after his administration proposed a fresh 25 percent tariff on Brazilian goods, Trump praised him publicly . Flavio asked Washington to postpone the tariffs until after the voting period, but it was too late: a Datafolha poll found that 52 percent of Brazilians saw the tariffs as an effort to help his campaign, but ultimately hurting the Brazilian economy.
Until 2030, Brazil and Mexico, the two largest economies in Latin America, will be governed by center-left leaders, both of whom refuse to pick a clear side between Washington and Beijing. For a doctrine premised on sorting the hemisphere into aligned and unaligned camps, this is a strategic setback for Trump, precisely at a moment where the leader faces low approval rates at home.
Beijing’s Geoeconomic Influence in the Region Is Growing
For China, Brazil is now a strategic partner. In 2025 it was the single largest destination for Chinese outbound investment worldwide, absorbing 10.9 percent of the total, according to the China-Brazil Business Council (CEBC). Chinese investment in China reached $6.1 billion, up 45 percent, far outpacing both Brazil’s overall foreign direct investment (FDI) growth of 4.8 percent and China’s global outbound growth of 1.3 percent .
Overall Brazil accounts for almost two thirds of China’s FDI in South America, with a total stock of $85.5 billion , distributed across 355 projects, between 2007-2025.
China continues to invest heavily in Brazil’s electricity sector, spanning renewable generation and transmission . Automotive investment rose 66 percent to $965 million as BYD began production at the former Ford complex in Camaçari, Bahia (Northeastern Brazil), and Great Wall Motors at the former Mercedes-Benz plant in Iracemápolis, São Paulo. Geely has sealed an alliance with Renault do Brasil and plans local production in Paraná (Southern Brazil) this year.
Beyond investment, bilateral trade hit a record $171 billion in 2025. China bought nearly 80 percent of Brazil’s soybean exports. These ties survived even Jair Bolsonaro’s hostile rhetoric. But a Flavio government that owed its political capital to Washington would have faced intense pressure to slow Chinese investment, and it would have inherited brand-new legal tools to do so (more on this below).
After his loss, Flavio Bolsonaro immediately fled Brazil, heading secretly to the United States via Argentina, amid fears of being convicted of ties to money laundering schemes.
Brazil and the Race for Technology and Critical Minerals
Lula signed Law 15.506/2026 on September 16, creating Brazil’s first National Policy on Critical and Strategic Minerals (PNMCE) and a council, the CIMCE, attached to the presidency. The stakes for investors are considerable: Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves and leads global niobium production, with newly found lithium and nickel reserves.
China still controls roughly 90 percent of rare earth processing and magnet manufacturing and the United States was seeking to secure privileged access to exploration of this sector in the Brazilian market.
The new law has two main aspects: promotion and regulation. The first key is promotion in an industrial policy style. Brazil’s government will provide up to 7 billion Brazilian real in support for firms aiming to raise production and processing of critical minerals, as well as tax credits of up to 1 billion real a year between 2030 and 2034, tied to value-adding and processing on Brazilian soil.
The second aspect is regulation. The newly formed council, led by the president, must approve direct or indirect changes of control in companies holding rights to critical minerals, as well as international supply agreements that could affect Brazil’s economic or geopolitical security.
On paper, this created a screening mechanism that can be used as a hurdle for Chinese state capital, depending on the elected administration. A senior official at the Ministry of Mines and Energy said in October that scrutiny would concentrate on business groups or financing backed by foreign governments, while purely domestic deals may be exempt.
Today, the most visible foreign investors in Brazilian rare earths are American. In April 2026, USA Rare Earth acquired the Serra Verde Mining Complex , Brazil’s only commercial producer of rare earths, for $2.8 billion, in a deal backed by the U.S. government, including $565 million in direct funding from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.
Meanwhile, between 2024-2025 three Chinese state-owned enterprises invested more than $1.2 billion in acquisitions of copper, nickel, niobium and lithium mines in Brazil. BYD has held lithium rights in Minas Gerais region since 2023.
Under Lula, the CIMCE is likely to wield screening as an industrial policy filter, asking how much value stays in Brazil. The new law rewards precisely what Chinese firms can offer and Washington struggles to: refining know-how, battery materials capacity, and captive demand from EV plants already operating in Brazil. Under a Flavio government, however, the same powers could easily have been aligned with Washington’s geoeconomic

articles.title_orig: Everything Apple Announced This Week: All About OLED, MacBooks And A Touchscreen
articles.title_zh: Everything Apple Announced This Week: All About OLED, MacBooks And A Touchscreen
articles.content_orig:
In addition to the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display at a "Pro and Tell" event in LA, this week brought us an OLED iPad mini and M6 MBP.
Apple wasn't done with its product reveals for the fall after unveiling the iPhone Duo , iPhone 18 Pro models and an array of smart home devices . Nor could it wait until the third event of the season, dubbed "Pro and Tell," to show off more gear.
The company got a string of announcements underway on Monday with the reveal of the long-awaited OLED iPad mini. Tuesday brought us an M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. Then, on Wednesday, Apple unveiled its long-anticipated touchscreen MacBook Pro.
Elsewhere, Apple released the latest versions of its operating systems. Among other things, those added more Siri AI features and made the assistant available in more languages. The company updated Apple Creator Studio with more AI features and creative tools as well.
Here's an overview of everything Apple announced this week.
It feels like we've been waiting for forever for Apple to put an OLED display in the iPad mini but that day has finally arrived. The new display has double the peak brightness of the one on the previous model at 1,200 nits, and it has a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The base storage remains the same at 128GB, though if you opt for 256GB or 512GB of storage, you can snag a variant with a nano-texture glass display. That'll cost you extra, naturally.
The company managed to squeeze in a larger screen — an 8.5-inch display rather than the 8.3-inch one in the previous model — without increasing the size of the tablet. In fact, the new iPad mini is slightly narrower than the last one, at 5.22 inches vs. 5.3 inches. It's lighter as well, with the Wi-Fi model coming in at 0.56 pounds (compared with 0.65 pounds last time) and the 5G variant weighing 0.58 pounds (versus 0.66 pounds). The latter, by the way, now boasts Apple's C2 modem, which is said to deliver up to 50 percent faster data speeds than the previous iPad mini. There's also Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity thanks to the N1 chip.
The OLED iPad mini — the eighth generation of the device — runs on the A20 Pro, the same chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Apple says the SoC is capable of running large language models locally, in case you're into that kind of thing. Otherwise, the tablet should be notably faster than earlier models. It supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI as well, of course. The chipset also boasts a 7-core GPU — two more cores than the A17 Pro, which powered the last-gen iPad mini.
On the camera front, there's a 12MP Center Stage lens on front of the tablet, which Apple has finally shifted to the landscape edge on the iPad mini. However, there's still no Face ID. The 12MP camera on the rear supports 4K 60fps video capture and Smart HDR 4.
The 8th-gen iPad mini has a sealed enclosure to help protect it from the elements. The tablet has an IP67 rating, meaning that it should withstand dust and being immersed in a meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes, though I would advise against intentionally submerging your iPad mini.
As for battery life, Apple says that should be roughly the same as last time. The company says the new iPad mini should run for up to 10 hours when you're watching video or surfing the web over Wi-Fi. That drops down to nine hours if you're browsing over a cellular connection. If you have at least a 35W power adaptor, you'll be able to recharge the battery to 50 percent of its capacity in 30 minutes, Apple says.
The most interesting thing to me about this iPad mini is that it has Apple's first Acoustic Display, which the company says helps it deliver "an even better audio experience." It claims the tablet offers more volume and "punchier bass" thanks to woofers that "are paired through the display." Apple added that "custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs." I'm definitely curious to find out how all of that sounds in practice.
Inevitably, the latest iPad mini comes with a price hike. It starts at $699, which is $150 more than the previous model after Apple increased the price of that in June . Pre-orders are now open and the tablet will hit shelves on November 6.
On Tuesday, Apple gave the iMac and MacBook Pro spec bumps. The desktop and laptop now each have the M6 chipset , which recently debuted in the Mac mini .
Let's start with the new iMac . Apple says the M6's dual 16-core neural engine enables it to deliver up to five times faster on-device AI performance (for Siri AI, Apple Intelligence and local LLMs) than the previous-gen iMac from 2024 , which had the M4 chipset. The M6 is said to deliver up to 1.5 times faster performance than the M4 for daily tasks, up to two times faster graphics performance (for photo editing etc.) and up to two times higher gaming performance with ray tracing.
The base-level M6 has 10 CPU cores (two super, three performance and two efficiency cores) and a 10-core CPU, compared with eight of each in the M4. There's the option to have a 12-core M6, in which case your desktop will have four Thunderbolt 4 ports instead of the two that the base model has. The four-port model has a nano-texture glass option as well.
Elsewhere, Apple has introduced its N1 networking chip to the iMac. As such, the computer has support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity. It also has the option to add a 2.5Gb Ethernet port, an upgrade from gigabit Ethernet on the M4 iMac.
Specs otherwise are the same as last time. You'll still get a 24-inch 4.5K Super Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six‑speaker Dolby Atmos system, at least 16GB of RAM and 256GB of base storage. The dimensions are identical too, though the M6 iMac is a touch lighter than the previous gen at 9.7 pounds (versus 9.74 pounds). Don't expect any changes to the color options either — the new iMac is still available in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.
One other thing that's staying the same? The starting price, at least after the $200 increase that Apple gave the M4 iMac over the summer. The new model starts at $1,499, and the four-port version will run you at least $1,699. Pre-orders are open and you'll be able to pick one up in store on November 6.
The latest 14-inch MacBook Pro has the 12-core version of the M6 chipset and the N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. Those appear to be the only spec changes this time.
Compared with the previous-gen 14-inch MBP, which had an M5 SoC, Apple says the M6 model offers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads. It's said to deliver up to 1.3 faster rendering performance with ray tracing in Blender, up to 1.2 times faster image-processing performance in Affinity and up to 1.3 faster project build performance for compiling code in Xcode.
It doesn't seem like this will be a massive upgrade for folks with an M5 model. However, if you have an older MacBook Pro (or really need those incremental improvements from the previous gen), it might be worth making the switch.
Either way, creatives might want to take note of all the updates that are rolling out for Apple Creative Studio . Apple has given Final Cut Pro a long-awaited quality-of-life upgrade by letting you pull clips from the primary storyline and place them anywhere on the timeline, which seems like very basic functionality to have! MotionVFX is integrated into the app on Mac as well, so you'll have thousands of elements at your fingertips for your video edits.
If you have a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence and is set to US English, Logic Pro has an "intelligent assistant" powered by OpenAI that's available in beta. The app has an an enhanced Stem Splitter that can now separate drums as well. In addition, Keynote, Pages and Numbers now have a chatbot you can use to adjust presentations, documents and spreadsheets.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court wants to hear from Hillary Clinton before deciding on Trump’s petition
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court wants to hear from Hillary Clinton before deciding on Trump’s petition
articles.content_orig:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday told Hillary Clinton to respond to a petition from President Donald Trump that seeks to revive his lawsuit that claims she conspired with others ahead of the 2016 election to “weave a false narrative” that his campaign colluded with Russia .
Lower courts have rejected Trump’s suit, and he wants the justices to intervene. Clinton and her civil co-defendants initially waived their right to respond to Trump’s petition. Had the court not requested a response, that would have all but guaranteed that the petition was headed for denial.
Although the response request is good news for Trump, it doesn’t necessarily signal the court is certain to grant review of his petition. Because it takes only one justice to request a response, it’s unclear how much of an appetite there is on the nine-member bench to take this one up. Response requests don’t specify how many justices asked for the response, nor do they explain why the response was requested.
It takes four justices to grant review.
Clinton’s brief opposing Trump’s petition is now due Nov. 27. The justices will consider in a private conference at some point after that whether to grant review. The Democrat recently made news for endorsing expanding the number of justices who sit on the court that currently has a 6-3 majority of Republican appointees.
Trump argues that he put off bringing the civil case during his first term due to his presidential responsibilities at the time. In his petition , his personal lawyers cast high court review as “necessary to protect the Presidency, and to prevent judicial disagreement from becoming a license to punish its advocates.”
The lower courts have rejected Trump so far. A conservative appeals court upheld a district judge’s ruling that dismissed his suit and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against him, Alina Habba and her law firm. The appellate panel noted that many of his and Habba’s legal claims “were indeed frivolous.”
The panel also cited the Supreme Court’s 1997 ruling in Clinton v. Jones that said Bill Clinton couldn’t avoid judicial process in civil litigation while he was in office. “If a president can be haled into court, he cannot be excused from suing to enforce his rights,” the panel reasoned.
In his Supreme Court petition, Trump’s lawyers maintained that there is an important distinction between suing and being sued. They said the Clinton v. Jones precedent “permitted another citizen’s suit against the President while requiring respect for the Presidency; it did not require him to pursue his own claims while in office or lose them.”
They also cited the Supreme Court’s 2024 criminal immunity ruling in Trump’s favor to argue that courts can’t make presidents decide whether to initiate personal litigation while in office. His lawyers are pressing that position as the president pursues an array of personal litigation , including multiple defamation claims .
This case is not Trump’s only pending bid to persuade the justices to revive personal litigation that he has lost in lower courts, nor is it the only one to invoke the presidency in doing so.
Although the Supreme Court has already rejected one of his two petitions seeking to reverse his defamation losses against the writer E. Jean Carroll, his second petition is awaiting a response from Carroll before the justices decide whether to grant or likewise deny that one. There, too, his lawyers cite the criminal immunity ruling in seeking to overturn the $83.3 million judgment Carroll won for statements Trump made during his first term.
The president is also pressing a defamation appeal against CNN over the network’s use of the phrase “big lie” regarding his 2020 election claims. That petition is awaiting a response from CNN, which, as happened in this Clinton litigation, the court requested after the network waived its right to respond.

articles.title_orig: China-Vatican deal has imperfections, Vatican’s foreign minister says
articles.title_zh: China-Vatican deal has imperfections, Vatican’s foreign minister says
articles.content_orig:
Archbishop Paul Gallagher acknowledged the agreement’s challenges in a meeting with journalists in Rome.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican’s secretary for relations with states and international organizations, acknowledged the challenges of the Vatican-China deal on Tuesday.
Speaking at an event with journalists in Rome, the British diplomat responded to questions regarding the agreement, Pope Leo XIV’s health, and calls for a ceasefire in the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war.
The full text of the 2018 agreement between China and the Holy See has never been made public. Under the publicly understood terms of the agreement, the pope retains final authority over episcopal appointments in China and may reject candidates proposed by Beijing. The Holy See, for its part, agreed not to appoint bishops without the Chinese government’s prior approval.
As reported by Reuters , Gallagher said that, regarding the agreement, its imperfections were visible.
“Itʼs not easy, the dialogue is not easy,” Gallagher said. “The imperfections of the agreement are ⁠evident, but ​there is a commitment to persevere in dialogue ... and that is what will ​continue to happen.”
He also answered questions regarding a potential visit from Leo to the U.S., saying that it could happen “in the not too distant future.”
Regarding the pope’s Oct. 13 surgery and subsequent recovery, Gallagher described it as a “bit of a game changer” and a revelation of the pope’s mortality, as with every human being.
“[The pope] is a poor mortal like the rest of ​us,” Gallagher said.
In August, Gallagher traveled to Russia to discuss the country’s ongoing war with Ukraine with senior officials. He told journalists that he did not believe the Vatican was involved in discussions of the ceasefire between the two nations.

articles.title_orig: Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform
articles.title_zh: Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform
articles.content_orig:
Google today announced the Connected Apps Platform as a “unified way for more app developers to bring their capabilities directly into Gemini and Search.”
Existing third-party Connected Apps let you access Adobe, Dropbox, Instacart, OpenTable, Ticketmaster, and other services — now numbering over 50 — from the Gemini app. Google also announced a new Calm integration that will be available in the coming weeks. These @-integrations join first-party offerings like Google Workspace, Photos, and YouTube. To date, the creation process has required working closely with Google.
Google is now expanding availability on multiple fronts, starting with the Connected Apps Platform. It’s billed as a way to “build once and reach high-intent users.” Developers need to have a cloud-hosted MCP server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs. They then register, test, and submit their Connected Apps using the new Google Connected Console. This new website lets them track traffic, latency, and error rates, as well as control brand identity.
In addition to the Gemini app, Google will soon make existing Connected Apps available in Search. Developers can “choose whether [their app] will go live in Search, the Gemini app, or both.” As part of the recent redesign, the Gemini app gained a new Customize page .
Developers can sign up for the preview at developers.google.com/connected-apps . Google is opening up access in phases over the coming months.

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at his rape and sex assault trial
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at his rape and sex assault trial
articles.content_orig:
Russell Brand took the stand in his criminal trial in London on Wednesday, denying all accusations against him and revealing that he was not able to convince anyone to testify on his behalf.
He was called by his lawyer, Ian Winter KC, as the first and only witness as his defense began to lay out its case, according to Sky News . Winter began by asking Brand if he had committed each of the alleged offenses he is being accused of, to which he repeatedly replied: “No.” Questioned about his prominence in the mid-2000s, Brand said that his marriage to Katy Perry in 2010 brought about “staggering fame.”
Brand then revealed that not a single person with relevant information agreed to testify on his behalf in the trial. “My entire life has been consumed by these allegations,” he told the Southwark Crown Court. “I have devoted myself to these matters.”
He called the 2023 Channel 4 documentary about him “devastating” and claimed that he was not able to visit his sick son in the hospital because he had been publicly accused of rape. “The reason given by Great Ormond Street Hospital when my son was receiving open heart surgery and subsequent treatment was due to the material published,” he said, according to Sky News.
On Tuesday, judge Mr Justice Bennathan reduced one of Brand’s seven charges from indecent assault to attempted indecent assault, telling jurors that there was “insufficient evidence” regarding an alleged 2001 incident involving a MTV employee. He has also been charged with three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and has pleaded not guilty to all charges. The case involves six female plaintiffs, all of whom are given automatic lifelong anonymity according to U.K. law, and relates to alleged offenses that occurred between 1999 and 2009.
Outside the courthouse on Wednesday, Brand told journalists (via Sky News): “Due to the circumstances of today, I think it would be inappropriate for me to say anything other than I am very grateful that today’s a day for truth and justice and we are blessed that as yet we have a system that can accommodate such things.” He was accompanied by his wife, Laura Gallacher.
On the stand, Brand was then questioned by the defense about the first allegation, concerning a woman who alleged he raped her at the 1999 Labour party conference. After meeting at his cabaret show, Brand said the woman “suggested we go to her hotel room” and he thought there may be a “possibility of sex.” In the room, he said there was “messing about, some kissing on the body and sex with a condom.” Asked about her claim that he forced her to take the photos, Brand responded: “I don’t know how you can make someone take photographs.” Further questioned on the importance of consent, he said, “Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary, and in many ways more important than sex itself.”
Moving on to the second accusation, involving a woman who claims Brand grabbed her and tried to pull her into a toilet while she was working at MTV in 2001, Brand said he has no recollection of the alleged incident. Regarding the third complainant, who alleged Brand squeezed her breasts at a party in Soho in 2004 and then orally raped her in a toilet, he said he was introduced to her by the host of the party as a “bird” who “really wants to meet you.” He said he “absolutely” did not grab her breasts and said the toilet she claimed he orally raped her in “was unsuitable for me to meet the goal… of getting it off.” He also denied the fourth woman’s allegation, who claimed he allegedly pushed her against a wall and “aggressively” kissed her while she was working at Capital Radio in 2004/2005.
Regarding the fifth accuser, who alleged that Brand anally raped her in 2009 after they had consensual vaginal sex, he claimed that she did not say “no” or tell him to stop. He also said he believed that taking off his condom before the alleged anal rape was a “consensual act,” according to Sky News. He denied sexually assaulting the sixth complainant as well, who alleged she was forced to give him a massage at work in 2009.
“I’m innocent,” Brand said as the defense’s questioning ended.
The prosecution has set out its case over the past two weeks. In her opening statement at the start of the trial, Riel Karmy-Jones KC called Brand a “predator,” adding that he was “ruthless and calculated” with an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact.
Cross-examining Brand on Wednesday, Karmy-Jones asked him if he blames the women who have come forward against him, and Brand said he does not. He also denied that he had a “goal” of sleeping with 5,000 women, as he allegedly told a friend at the time; however, he admitted to being “obsessed” with sex when he was younger. Asked if he ever said he wouldn’t leave a woman alone until he slept with her, Brand referenced a quote from Woody Allen, the director who has also faced his own allegations. “That sounds specifically like a riff on a Woody Allen joke, when he said, ‘The only advice my dad ever gave me on his death bed was always try and fuck the waitress,'” Brand said, adding: “It was a joke.”
Questioned about the specific alleged offenses, Brand responded often with “I don’t remember” or “I have no recollection.” Asked by Karmy-Jones if he is being “selective” with his memory, Brand said he was doing his “best” to remember the events being discussed. He later added, when asked about inconsistencies in his police statements, that hearing the complainants’ allegations during the trial has caused an “escalating recollection” of events.
“It’s been a deeply traumatic episode of my life,” he said. “I’ve focused on it at the expense of my marriage, my children and health. I ask your forgiveness — well, not your forgiveness. I recognize that this recollection includes small details which are inconsistent, and I recognize that.”
Asked generally about his past behavior, via Sky News, Brand said he was “in the position of fame” and “misused that commodity very selfishly,” which was “wrong in retrospect.”
“As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong,” he continued. “I do recognize I have been a very determined and focused man … With women — of course, which is the subject of my trial — I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless, philandering and idiocy.”
He later restated that “not guilty is my plea to all the charges on the indictment.”
Brand’s defense will continue on Thursday. The jury is expected to start deliberating a verdict on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Palantir Board Member Cofounded Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner’s Blood-Testing Startup
articles.title_zh: Palantir Board Member Cofounded Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner’s Blood-Testing Startup
articles.content_orig:
Billy Evans has spent the past week as the breakout character of the year’s most talked-about documentary. Now attention is turning to his day job.
Evans, the longtime partner of convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, runs Haemanthus, an Austin-based startup that says it can use lasers to detect disease in blood, saliva, and urine. Interest in the company has surged since A24 released You Can See Everything , Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about the couple, on Oct. 16.
Haemanthus has reportedly raised as much as $20 million and holds at least one granted patent. What it doesn’t have, at least publicly, is a product customers can buy or published data showing its technology works. It has also lost its chief technology officer .
Set aside the “Theranos 2.0” jokes, and a more basic business question remains: What has Haemanthus actually built?
Evans, 34, is a grandson of William and Anne Evans, who founded Evans Hotels in San Diego in 1953. The privately held, family-owned company operates three resorts in Southern California. But in an Oct. 1 statement, Evans Hotels said Billy Evans is neither an employee nor a shareholder .
Evans graduated from MIT in 2015 with a degree in economics. After a stint at LinkedIn, he worked as a special projects manager at Luminar Technologies, a lidar startup building sensors for self-driving cars, from 2017 until January 2019, according to Forbes . His LinkedIn profile has since been scrubbed of every job except Haemanthus. Luminar filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2025, nearly seven years after Evans left.
Evans met Holmes at a party in 2017, when Theranos was already engulfed in scandal. They have two children, William, 5, and Invicta, 3. Evans refers to Holmes as his wife, but Holmes told People that the couple never legally married. “Maybe we’ll get married someday, but our bond is more than a piece of paper,” she said.
Evans has listed himself as Haemanthus’s CEO since October 2022. According to marketing materials reviewed by the New York Times last year, the company’s device uses a laser to scan biological samples “on a molecular level,” identify biomarkers such as glucose and hormones within seconds, and use AI to detect cancer and infections.
The underlying technique, Raman spectroscopy, is not new. Shining light on a sample and reading the signal that scatters back is a long-established way to identify chemicals. Forensic investigators use handheld Raman devices to identify suspected drugs at crime scenes, and labs can analyze substances through plastic bags or glass without opening them.
Blood is a much harder problem. The molecules researchers want to detect are often present in tiny amounts, so their signals are faint. Other components in blood can produce stronger signals that drown them out, according to a scientific review published in Applied Spectroscopy .
That approach is also what separates Haemanthus from Theranos. Holmes’s company claimed it could run conventional lab tests on a miniaturized machine using a few drops of blood. “Theranos attempted to miniaturize existing tests,” Haemanthus wrote on X in May 2025, describing its own approach as fundamentally different.
A Raman spectroscopy patent assigned to Haemanthus and granted in January 2025 names two inventors, one of them former CTO Joseph LaChapelle, according to Forbes . Several of the startup’s early staffers, including LaChapelle, worked with Evans at Luminar, NPR reported . Eric Potma, a UC Irvine chemistry professor who consults for the company, told Wired that the concept isn’t pulled out of thin air, though he declined to go into detail because of his advisory role.
A patent, however, does not establish that a test can accurately diagnose patients.
Haemanthus plans to start with veterinary testing before pursuing human applications. That market is far less regulated. The FDA does not require premarket approval for devices intended for animals, though it can take action against misbranded or adulterated products.
According to investor materials the Times reviewed last year, Haemanthus initially raised $3.5 million from friends and family. In spring 2025 it began approaching wealthy investors in Austin and the San Francisco Bay Area for another $15 million. The materials described an eventual wearable device for humans that would take three years and $70 million to develop. Wired has since reported that the company has received as much as $20 million.
A person who spoke with Evans this spring told Forbes that Evans said early Palantir employees had invested.
The company has yet to launch a commercial product or disclose independently validated diagnostic results.
LaChapelle told Forbes he left in March. “I resigned on March 16, 2026, due to a conflict of interest associated with a stealth startup I had founded prior to Haemanthus,” he said, declining to elaborate.
Evans has told it differently. The same person who spoke with Evans this spring told Forbes that Evans said he had let the CTO go. That person also recalled Evans describing the company as “Theranos 2.0,” a label Haemanthus has publicly rejected. Evans did not respond to Forbes’ s request for comment.
Holmes is serving an 11-year sentence for defrauding Theranos investors at a federal prison camp in Bryan, Texas, roughly a two-hour drive from Austin.
Citing two sources with direct knowledge, NPR reported in May 2025 that Holmes had been advising Evans from prison, though the nature of that advice was unclear. Haemanthus denied it on X , saying Holmes had “zero involvement” and “no role, now or future.” Wired reported that Holmes’s name does not appear in Haemanthus’s incorporation documents.
The documentary muddies that picture. It shows Evans and Holmes on fundraising calls and discussing a medical-testing venture, and Evans tells Fielder, “The idea is to put the band back together and do it all again.” Forbes noted it’s unclear whether those calls were for Haemanthus or another venture. A source close to Evans told New York magazine that the project in the film was separate from Haemanthus. According to that source, it aimed to make medical testing cheaper without conventional chemical methods and was shelved when a panel of tests still cost several hundred dollars.
Evans has acknowledged the film may backfire. Speaking at the All-In Summit before he had seen the finished cut, he said, “I might think this is like the dumbest thing I’ve ever done.”
The documentary reveals that Evans asked for a share of its profits, a request that worried the filmmakers about their independence. Fielder says they reluctantly agreed. A postscript says Evans ultimately decided not to accept payment.
That may not be the end of it. Page Six Hollywood reported on Friday, citing unnamed sources, that Evans has been seeking Hollywood legal representation over a possible cut. One prominent litigator reportedly declined to take the case, and a source said Evans might donate any proceeds to charity.
The film has put Holmes back in the spotlight. Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz and Bad Blood author John Carreyrou have both weighed in, and Fortune has questioned whether her new persona distracts from the real story . It has also drawn far more scrutiny to Evans and Haemanthus. The company has yet to publicly show that its technology can reliably detect disease. It also remains unclear when its veterinary device will reach the market or how close its larger ambitions are to reality.

articles.title_orig: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
articles.title_zh: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
articles.content_orig:
LOS ANGELES—Apple today announced and gave a first glimpse of its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years. As rumored, it includes an OLED display and, for the first time on macOS, a touchscreen—a change Apple has long debated. (Former CEO Steve Jobs famously was opposed.)
Apple’s demonstration video showed users interacting with applications by reaching up to touch the screen, including file dragging and multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom. It does not appear to be a 2-in-1 convertible design, though; all the footage was of people reaching up to touch the screen in a normal laptop configuration.
The OLED display (which Apple is, of course, calling the PROLED XDR) seems to be the real highlight here, compared to earlier models: It can achieve 2,000 nits in terms of maximum brightness, and Apple says it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. References were made to burn-in protection, but details on which approach it’s taking for that weren’t yet shared. The display retains the 120 Hz variable refresh rate of its predecessors.
Beyond that, the design is largely similar to the existing one, but there are a few notable differences. First, it’s much lighter. Apple said when announcing it that the 14-inch model is just 3 pounds, down around half a pound from the previous model, depending on configuration.
Second, the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by the small black cutout that Apple calls the Dynamic Island. Presumably it works similarly to the one we’ve seen on the iPhone, expanding or contracting to show live activities and other information.
Finally, there’s a retro throwback: The Apple logo on the back of the lid glows like the logo on MacBooks of yore.
In terms of specs, this refresh includes the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips—the same ones in the previous refresh. The M6 series has already arrived in other Macs, but it seems Apple is skipping them for this refresh; there were previously reports that Apple planned to hold off on updating the chip until the M7 series, which could have significant improvements for AI performance, just like the recently released A20 Pro chip for the iPhone does.
Memory configurations top out where they did in previous MacBook Pro models with M5 Max: up to 128GB of RAM. That said, storage can now go up to 16TB—if you can afford it.
Preorders start today, and the device will reach consumers on November 6. As expected, the price is the catch. The M5 Pro-equipped 14-inch model starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. But if you want the M5 Max, you’re looking at a $4,499 starting point for the 14-inch, and $4,799 for the 16-inch—and that’s not accounting for any potential RAM or storage upgrades.

articles.title_orig: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
articles.title_zh: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.
The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.
He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate . Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack .
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.
Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.
"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.
"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.
"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.
"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.
It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.
Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled .
Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.
"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."
Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.
"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.
At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.
Burnham's comments at Prime Minister's Questions came as a letter emerged addressed to his Cabinet ministers, asking them to be "aligned and disciplined" around the summit.
"It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process," he wrote in a letter on Wednesday.
He said he hoped the summit led to "some important, concrete steps" and he would set out the next steps "to consider the UK's long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan".
"Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote," he said.
"Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality."
Any "fundamental change" to this relationship "would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next Parliament," he added.

articles.title_orig: Iran war’s cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
articles.title_zh: Iran war’s cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
articles.content_orig:
A continuous world cruise came to an unexpected end in Cambodia on Tuesday, forcing passengers to disembark as the operator suspended operations due to âextraordinary increases in fuel costs.â
Villa Vie Residences, which operates the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey, said in a news release that it would evaluate restructuring and recapitalization options. The ship sold permanent residences starting at about $120,000, as well as five-year residences, a three-year voyage and short-term rentals.
The announcement said that fuel expenses had shot up from an average of $1,800 a month per cabin to more than $6,000 â a cost that could not be passed on to passengers.
âSince the conflict [in Iran] began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,â the companyâs statement said. âThose measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.â
Villa Vie said it was working with the passengers to find âtemporary living arrangements.â
The company did not immediately answer questions about how many passengers and crew were on board or what will happen to them.
Randy Cassingham, a writer who has lived on the ship since late 2024, wrote on his site Residential Cruising that passengers received a message after 7 a.m. telling them they had to disembark by 2 p.m.
He said in an email that he had to find his own hotel, and was not aware of the company helping anyone find a place to stay or paying for accommodations.
âThe evacuated residents are exhausted both physically and emotionally,â he wrote on the website.
U.S. military officials estimate that the Trump administrationâs war with Iran has cost more than $47 billion through mid-October, a rise of more than $3 billion over the past several weeks, according to a document reviewed by The Washington Post.
The total includes $29 billion in munitions that have been fired by U.S. forces since the conflict began eight months ago, the document shows. The destruction of other weapons platforms, such as fighter jets, has cost $6 billion, it says.
The latest figures do not account for damage to U.S. bases in the region, especially facilities in the Persian Gulf, which have been battered by Iranian drones and ballistic missiles.
The estimate was compiled by U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East. It marks the militaryâs latest and most detailed tally of the Iran warâs financial costs. Central Command last projected that the war had cost at least $43.6 billion through early September .
The rising expense has forced the Pentagon to shift billions of dollars from within its existing budget to cover shortfalls caused by the conflict as the military has had to rush troops and equipment to the Middle East and keep them there for months on end.
Per the most recent estimate, the Air Force had spent about $7.6 billion to sustain the military operation, whereas the Army and the Navy had spent $2 billion and $1.45 billion, respectively.
The Iran war, which was initiated by the Trump administration in tandem with Israel on Feb. 28, has proved deeply unpopular with the American public, polling shows. It has emerged as a central issue in next weekâs midterm elections, with voters frustrated by the soaring cost of gas and other goods linked to Tehranâs closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
At the outset of the conflict, President Donald Trump predicted that hostilities would be over in about five weeks. His administration has been unable to secure a lasting ceasefire on terms that the president finds favorable to American interests, however, and he has threatened to resume attacks on Iran after the midterms.
Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska endorsed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in the stateâs governorâs race Tuesday.
âOur future is too important to be hamstrung by partisan divisions,â Murkowski said in a statement. âAlaska needs a serious conversation about our fiscal future, as well as a focus on the cost of energy and growing our economy.â
In a statement, Kreiss-Tomkins said he was honored by Murkowskiâs endorsement, adding that the stateâs unique priorities require âcooperation, not political conflict.â
When contacted by text about the endorsement, Kreiss-Tomkins responded with flexed-arm and rocket emojis.
Kreiss-Tomkins is the leading candidate based on public polling in a four-way race against three Republicans. Bernadette Wilson, a business executive, is running with President Donald Trumpâs backing. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting.
Murkowski, who depends on independent and crossover voters in her own races, endorsed Democrat Mary Peltola in her 2022 and 2024 races for the U.S. House (though she endorsed Peltolaâs Republican opponent in this yearâs Senate race).
As a state representative, Kreiss-Tomkins worked to create a bipartisan governing coalition, which controls both chambers of the state legislature. He served in the state House from 2013 to 2023, winning a district that voted for Trump.
Alaska Republicans have gone after Murkowski in the past, including in her 2022 primary and in 2010, when she won as a write-in candidate. Wilson campaigned against Murkowski in 2010 and blasted her for endorsing Kreiss-Tomkins.
âGiven that Senator Lisa Murkowski abandoned Alaska values a long time ago, I am not surprised that she has endorsed âJust Keep Taxingâ JKT,â Wilson wrote on X.
DNA testing connected serial killer Ted Bundy to the death of another teenage girl in Utah more than 50 years ago, authorities said Tuesday.
The body of Melissa Ann Smith, 17, was discovered by hunters in October 1974, officials told a news conference.
For decades, Smithâs death remained a mystery â until earlier this year, when investigators in Utah County used DNA evidence to identify what they said was another Bundy victim, 17-year-old Laura Aime, whose body was found in November 1974.
The breakthrough prompted investigators in the Smith case to compare samples taken from both bodies, officials said.
The DNA evidence, âalongside evidence related to pattern, motive, means and opportunity, establishes that Ted Bundy was responsible for Melissa Ann Smithâs murder,â Summit County Attorney Margaret Olson said.
Bundy was executed in 1989 after confessing to the killings of at least 30 people. Bundy had confessed to Aimeâs death before his death, without providing any details, according to the Associated Press .
âThe voices and cherished memories of Melissa Ann Smith and Laura Ann Aime and others involved in these cases ring louder than the hate and sedition of the one who took their lives,â said Mike Reynolds, a sergeant with the Utah County Sheriffâs Office.
The most affordable electric vehicle I test-drove in Mexico City was born in China.
Chevroletâs roughly $24,400 Spark EUV seems tailor-made to take on the Dolphin Mini built by Chinaâs BYD, now the largest EV manufacturer in the world, selling for about $21,600 . Since my visit, Chevy has tried to undercut the Dolphin, selling it for about $21,100 if you include a trade-in and financing.
The Spark EUV is a rebadged Baojun Yep Plus, produced with GMâs partner SAIC and made in China, where it sells for the equivalent of less than $15,000 . General Motors did not respond to inquiries for this story.
The Spark is roomier than the Dolphin Mini Plus, with 54 percent more cargo space, but has only four seats, to the Dolphinâs five. It drives like a mini-Jeep: boxy and burly, with no finesse on the pavement but more power under the hood (100 hp, about a third more than the Dolphin Mini). articles.title_orig: Spain Train Crash Live Updates: At Least 68 Killed in High-Speed Train Collision, Officials Say
articles.title_zh: Spain Train Crash Live Updates: At Least 68 Killed in High-Speed Train Collision, Officials Say
articles.content_orig:
Toledo, Spain 6:07 p.m. Oct. 28
A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another in Spain on Wednesday morning near the central city of Toledo, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, officials said, in one of the deadliest train crashes in Spanish history.
The cause of the crash, which sent parts of both trains down a rural embankment, was not immediately clear. It was the second lethal crash this year involving the same two rail operators, and it was likely to deepen doubts about the security of Spain’s once-vaunted rail system.
In Spanish news reports, passengers described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.
The crash also came about a month ahead of national elections, and it had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s left-wing government.
Sixty-eight people were seriously injured in the crash, 15 of them critically, said Emiliano García-Page, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region.
Spain’s rail authority, the Adif, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company,” both covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville. Renfe is the national rail provider.
Initial reports suggested that the Iryo train was stopped on the tracks, and that the Renfe train barreled into it. Local news outlets reported that there were 397 passengers aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train.
Trains from the same operators collided on a southern line in January, leaving 46 people dead.
Isaac Barrientos, a spokesman for the government’s transportation ministry, said on Wednesday that initial reports indicated two carriages of the Iryo train had derailed. He said all traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia route had been suspended until further notice.
Mr. Sánchez visited the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon, saying that Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced. “If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” He declared three days of official mourning.
The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quickly voiced his own concern.
“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media soon after the crash. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.” His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.
Another deadly crash: In January , a northbound Iryo train derailed, two of its cars falling onto the opposite track, and a southbound Renfe train slammed into the carriages seconds later. An official report on what caused that lethal accident has not been released, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
A detailed account: In a news conference, Spain’s transportation minister described the events that he said preceded the crash on Wednesday.
José Bautista contributed reporting from the scene of the crash.
The U.S. State Department said in a statement that several U.S. citizens were among those injured in the crash. It did not provide information about their conditions.
Spain’s transportation minister said a train crash that killed dozens on Wednesday appeared to result from an “inexplicable” decision by traffic control operators to tell a high-speed train to continue its journey when another train was stopped farther along the tracks.
The minister, Óscar Puente, said he spent the morning watching a reconstruction of the accident and listening to audio recordings of communications between the control center in Madrid and the trains that crashed near Toledo, and he gave a detailed account of what he said preceded the crash at a news conference.
At about 8:30 a.m. local time, an automatic train control system near the site of the crash went down because of a computer failure, Mr. Puente said.
The system — known as the Linienzugbeeinflussung or LZB — dates to the 1960s and uses external technologies, such as track circuits and axel counters, to monitor the speed and position of trains. This information allows the system to automatically calculate when and how quickly a train can safely move forward. It then changes railroad signals accordingly.
On Wednesday, the safety system was inactive along a stretch of about 39 miles, or 63 kilometers, of tracks, so six trains traveling along that section were automatically stopped as a precaution. At that point, he said, the control center in Madrid took over.
“The control center communicated with the trains that had stopped, and at 8:36 a.m., the decision was made to allow the train that eventually collided with the stationary Iryo train to resume its journey as normal,” Mr. Puente said, referring to the private rail operator of the stopped train.
Traffic controllers working for Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s rail infrastructure, told the train that eventually rear-ended the other to restart its planned journey, Mr. Puente said, “despite there being another train ahead of it.”
The train that was hit from behind was believed to have received instructions from traffic operators to continue, he said, but for unknown reasons it did not proceed.
The moving train then hit the stationary train.
“And that is the origin of the accident that has taken place,” Mr. Puente said, adding that the moving train should have been stopped according to protocol.
The Madrid-Seville route is currently undergoing a modernization program that will replace the LZB system with the more modern European Rail Traffic Management System. Infrastructure officials hope that the new system will cut down on human error in signaling.
Mr. Puente also said that the driver of an uninvolved train tried to warn the control center of the dangers when its operators greenlit the rear train’s resumption of its journey. That driver told the control center operator that trains should proceed at lower-than-normal speeds. The operator, Mr. Puente said, acknowledged his error. “Oh, yes,” the operator replied.
K. R. Callaway contributed reporting.
When the crash happened, Yahadi Mohamed Maulud, 41, who lives in the nearby town of Yébenes, loaded his car with water bottles and rushed to help. “We found a massacre,” he said, describing torn limbs and a blood-covered woman searching for her brother. One of the first to arrive at the scene, he helped to move injured passengers and carry stretchers. Mr. Maulud said he often took the train himself to Madrid for business, but no more: “I’m never getting on that train again.”
So many people showed up at Madrid hospitals on Wednesday to donate blood for victims of the train crash that the authorities are asking citizens to wait until Thursday or the following days, when more donations will be needed.
“The response from the people of Madrid to the call for blood donations is overwhelming,” said Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid’s regional president. “Thank you, everyone.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke from the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon. “It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” he said, adding that while today’s accident and a fatal January crash on the same line seemed unrelated, Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced.
“If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” Spain needs to understand “what is the origin of this tragedy,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.title_zh: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.content_orig:
Study suggests the long-term fate of the solar system, including Earth, ‘may be far more complicated than predicted’, according to scientist
When a star like our sun grows old, it puffs up into a red giant that can gobble up its nearest planets.
But Chinese astronomers say they have found three solar systems where planets should have been eaten this way yet somehow survived – a puzzle that could change how scientists picture Earth’s distant future.
Using Nasa’s TESS space telescope, a team led by Qian Shengbang from Yunnan University showed that three Jupiter-like planets – each hugging an ageing star in the northern sky – had lived through their hosts ballooning out past them before shrinking back.

The leader of a Weil Gotshal & Manges practice group told his junior lawyers to look for employment, underscoring the firmâs perilous state as it consults with a restructuring lawyer.
Alex Lynch, who leads Weilâs capital markets group, communicated the news to associates in a group meeting Tuesday, a person familiar with the announcement said. He said the associates will remain employed for the time being and will continue to work on client matters, though he offered no specific timeline on their tenure, said the person, who requested anonymity to describe Weil communications.
Lynch and Weil did not respond to a request for comment.
The firmâs future existence is uncertain after a litany of partners fled, at least in part because of a lack of confidence in Weilâs leaders. Last month powerful corporate department chairman Michael Aiello moved toward an exit for rival Cravath, and a wide set of firm partners learned last weekend that incoming Weil leader Ramona Nee has decided not to take the job.
Davis Polk & Wardwell lawyers, including restructuring partner Brian Resnick, are advising Weil as it assesses its future, two people familiar with the matter said Tuesday. Resnick is head of Davis Polkâs liability management and special opportunities practice.
The storied New York-based firm, with more than 1,200 lawyers and $2 billion in revenue, has long been one of the USâs premier legal operations. It is renowned for its bankruptcy practice, acting as lead debtors counsel to Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc and Enron Corporation . It also was an M&A powerhouse, led by Aiello, who represented Fox Corp. on its $22 billion acquisition of Roku Inc.
Aielloâs departure along with others prompted the firm to explore its options, including a possible merger with another Big Law firm. But merger talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher fell through last week, raising questions as to whether a dissolution is the inevitable option.

articles.title_orig: RFK Jr. to Allow Broad Use of Unapproved Peptide Injections
articles.title_zh: RFK Jr. to Allow Broad Use of Unapproved Peptide Injections
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration on Wednesday acted to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . Food and Drug Administration scientific staffers had little input on the decision and opposed the changes, according to six people familiar with its development.
The draft policy posted online by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services covers a handful of injectable peptides promoted within the wellness industry for uses such as building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy. The government will take comments on the measure for two weeks.
The document, primarily written by HHS, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s long-standing mission of keeping unproven health products off the U.S. market, according to the people familiar with its development.
The people spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations.
The policy directs the FDA not to take action against specialty pharmacies that sell a half-dozen wellness peptides, including BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. Under FDA rules, those chemicals would otherwise be considered illegal drugs because they have not gone through the agency’s rigorous review process for safety and effectiveness.
People say these peptides hurt them. Their stories are muffled in MAHA’s push for medical freedom
According to the newly posted document, Kennedy determined the change “advances patient choice and freedom” while protecting people in the United States from peptides sold online that are often made from unscreened ingredients.
Kennedy has called himself a “big fan” of peptides and previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.
Lee Rosebush of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine said in an online post that HHS had taken “a huge step for patient and provider medical freedom.” The group, which is not a medical professional organization, represents people who prescribe or sell peptides.
The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers, which recently announced plans to offer wellness peptides once the government changed its policy. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth more than $2 billion.
Some peptides occur naturally in the human body, where they trigger hormones needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss .
The chemicals subject to the new policy have not been approved as safe and effective by the FDA. Still, they are promoted for a range of medical uses, including insomnia, anxiety, inflammatory conditions and migraines.
FDA advisers support easing restrictions on six peptides. Here’s what those drugs are and what happens next
Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official, noted that the FDA has approved rigorously tested drugs for all of those conditions.
As people “are diverted from those drugs toward this stuff, there will be more unnecessary pain and suffering,” said Lurie, who now leads the nonprofit Center for Science in the Public Interest.
He also questioned the timing of the change, days before the midterm election.
“This is a wink and nod to the MAHA faithful in the hope that they’ll show up at the polls,” said Lurie, referring to Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement.
A spokesperson for HHS said the agency is “confronting the risks of black-market peptides” by giving Americans “a more controlled alternative through licensed U.S. compounders.”
It is the latest example of Kennedy reshaping U.S. health policy in the MAHA mold. Some of the biggest figures in that movement sell peptide injections and supplements.
The decision is a stark break from FDA efforts to limit the availability of unproven wellness products, including peptides, stem cell therapies and dietary supplements , that make unsupported medical claims. But that approach put the agency at odds with Kennedy, who has publicly endorsed the benefits of all of those products.
Why Peptides Are So Popular | Chasing Life with Dr. Sanjay Gupta | CNN Audio
The policy published Wednesday is a step back from HHS’ original plan, according to two of the people who discussed its development.
HHS officials initially wanted the FDA to draft an official regulation that would add BPC-157 and other peptides to a list of drug substances deemed safe for use by compounding pharmacies, specialty businesses that make customized medications.
FDA officials warned that the agency’s scientific staffers had major safety concerns and would not support a regulation deeming the peptides safe. HHS officials moved to a different approach that directs the FDA not to enforce its rules against pharmacies that compound the substances.
FDA staffers ultimately provided technical assistance in drafting the HHS plan, including guardrails intended to improve safety, such as requiring pharmacies to use peptide ingredients from FDA-registered factories. Additionally, compounders are directed to collect information on side effects for safety analysis and verify the purity of peptides they use.
Lurie pointed out that the FDA, under federal law, does not have the authority to enforce those pharmacy requirements.
The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, which represents specialty pharmacies, said several details need to be clarified — including when the policy takes effect and how it will intersect with state pharmacy boards, who traditionally regulate pharmacists.
Decisions about regulating peptides and compounding pharmacies have almost always come from the FDA, which has an office dedicated to protecting U.S. consumers from unsafe or poor-quality compounded drugs.
The issue of compounding safety became a greater focus for the FDA after a deadly outbreak of fungal meningitis in 2012 was linked to contaminated injections from a Massachusetts compounding pharmacy. Once a niche business, compounding has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry, providing customized medications to doctors, clinics and hospitals.
It’s extremely rare for HHS to take the lead in drafting policies over the compounding industry, former FDA officials said. But federal law technically gives HHS authority over drug regulations, which are then delegated to the FDA.
Many in the U.S. who are using peptides today do not deal with a doctor or a pharmacy to get the injections, but often order vials online sold by chemical manufacturers based in China. Peptide sellers often try to skirt U.S. regulations by labeling their products as “for research use only” because the FDA does not regulate research chemicals.
In 2023, the FDA added more than a dozen peptides , including BPC-157 and TB-500, to its list of substances that should not be compounded due to risks of allergic reactions, kidney damage and tumor growth.
At a meeting in July , FDA staffers reiterated that more than half a dozen peptides brought forward for reconsideration remained unproven in terms of safety and effectiveness.
But a panel of outside experts voted to drop restrictions on the six peptides named in Wednesday’s document. The panel — selected by Kennedy’s HHS — included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field.

articles.title_orig: Xreal Aura is a new wired headset powered by Android XR
articles.title_zh: Xreal Aura is a new wired headset powered by Android XR
articles.content_orig:
The new wearable is the first of its kind to run on the Android XR platform.
The Android XR -powered Xreal Aura smartglasses are now available to buy, and if you order a pair before the end of the year you can get them for a discounted price.
Xreal first unveiled the Aura earlier this year at Google I/O . They're the first wired glasses to utilize the Google and Samsung co-developed XR (extended reality) OS, and run Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite chip.
Key to the Aura's appeal is their lightweight build. They weigh in at under 95g and look like a slightly chunkier version of a regular pair of glasses. The tradeoff is that they have to be tethered to a separate puck for battery and compute purposes. The external device also features a built-in trackpad and fingerprint sensor.
Xreal is pitching the Aura as a true do-it-all spatial computing wearable for work, entertainment, gaming and general AI-assisted tasks. Gemini is built into the OS, and you'll have access to 150 dedicated XR experiences out of the box, as well as all your standard day-to-day Google Play apps.
Among the made-for-XR games are the puzzler Cubism and a virtual version of the Fallout tabletop game Fallout: Factions . GameSir has worked with Xreal on a gamepad designed specifically for the Aura, which is equipped with a dedicated Gemini key that allows Google's chatbot to be immediately summoned mid-game. The company has also announced a wireless portable keyboard, and you can plug in your laptop or PC gaming handheld via USB-C. External devices appear in your spatial workspace alongside the built-in apps.
The Aura smartglasses have a 70-degree field-of-view, Micro-OLED displays and a resolution of 1200p at 120Hz. Bose handled tuning on the built-in open-ear speakers.
You can pick up the 12GB + 256GB model for $1,099 through December. It usually costs $1,279. The ordinarily $1,499 16GB + 512GB variant costs $1,299 for the remainder of 2026. Shipping is expected to begin in the middle of November.

articles.title_orig: US sanctions North Korean network accused of defrauding businesses
articles.title_zh: US sanctions North Korean network accused of defrauding businesses
articles.content_orig:
The Treasury Department has sanctioned 10 North Koreans and Russians powering Pyongyang's sprawling IT worker fraud enterprise — a state-run operation that churns out stolen identities, fake résumés and fake IT employees who infiltrate legitimate businesses. The hundreds of millions of dollars in proceeds are then used to fund North Korea's weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs.
The scheme is simple: North Korean operatives pose as legitimate IT professionals, secure jobs at unwitting U.S. and allied companies, and funnel the majority of their pay back to the regime. Once inside corporate networks, these workers can also access sensitive data, deploy malware and even extort their employers.
In diving into the global web of handlers, financial intermediaries and money launderers bolstering the fake identities, investigators discovered key parts of that machinery operating in Russia. Among those designated Wednesday is Russian national Vitold Viktorovich Obertas, an intermediary who has facilitated financial transactions for North Korean officials. Since January 2025, Obertas has processed nearly $2 million in cryptocurrency conversions and at least $1.25 million in additional currency transactions for DPRK officials.
The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control also sanctioned North Korean national Kim Ki Hyok, who leads an IT worker delegation in Russia and is responsible for monitoring the group's personnel and ensuring they meet financial targets. Since 2024, he has transferred nearly $500,000 in cryptocurrency on behalf of the delegation.
The Treasury also sanctioned the Russia-based, North Korean-controlled First Financial and Technical Development Center, which has generated millions for the regime by procuring highly trained IT workers for jobs in the U.S. and worldwide and operating cryptocurrency transfers behind the scenes. Six of its own operatives were designated alongside the organization.
All U.S.-linked property and interests in property of the designated persons have now been blocked, and Americans and U.S. residents are generally prohibited from engaging with them. The action goes beyond targeting individual fraudsters — it's an effort to begin dismantling the machinery that converts fraudulent employment into illicit revenue — and ultimately into funding for North Korea's weapons programs.
This story published first on CBS News at 12:31 p.m. on Oct. 28, 2026.
